In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data, the mixed model with repeated measures test is commonly employed to assess treatment differences. However, this approach's assumption of constant treatment effects over time can be unrealistic, resulting in lower than expected sensitivity to between-group differences at advanced stages of the disease. To address this limitation, the article suggests using a framework of natural cubic splines to incorporate time as a predictive factor in linear models and maintain compatibility with established software for statistical analysis. The article demonstrates this methodology's implementation in clinical research on Alzheimer's disease and showcases its enhancement of detectable treatment differences under both simulated and real-world data conditions. The article also highlights the recent progress in Alzheimer's disease modulation through targeting ApoE, the PICADIL-LD with accompanying data, and the implications of the findings for future research. The article finally discusses the computational and statistical underpinnings of the methodology, addressing potential issues of overfitting and loss of degrees of freedom in small-sample studies. To promote the widespread adoption of this methodology, the article recommends adding a time variable to the design of the study and specifying a natural cubic spline parameter in the model only when necessary, both actions resulting in no loss of degrees of freedom. Finally, the article provides step-by-step instructions for implementing the procedure in linear and generalized linear models in the PICADIL-LD software. The article concludes by acknowledging the potential extension of the methodology to other areas of neurodegenerative disease research. The suggested approach represents an important advancement in the use of statistical analysis for Alzheimer's disease research. Recent advancements in applying trajectory sampling techniques, such as Markov chain Monte Carlo, have enabled the exploration of complex multidimensional energy landscapes. Yet, for systems undergoing an arrhenius-type diffusion, these methods are inefficient due to frequent jumps between two peaks. A more practical approach involves a new global optimization technique that downsamples high-energy states and can accurately simulate barrier crossing events. It employs a dynamic potential approximation, modeling the energy landscape as a one-dimensional pathway that is periodically reoptimized. If the system's motion is arrhenius-like, this method ensures thorough exploration of the lowest-energy pathways. It has been theoretically validated for a standard model system and several others experiencing rate enhancements. Results demonstrate that this technique is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of multidimensional energy landscapes. It has been successfully applied to the simulation of multi-step pathways involving linear coupling between active sites. Furthermore, this technique has the capability of identifying the dominant transition routes as well as the rates associated with each mechanism from the simulated pathways. It has been applied to models of enzyme-assisted and catalyzed reactions, and the results show consistency with existing knowledge and suggest novel insights into the underlying reaction dynamics. For systems experiencing inner-sphere mediated reactions, the results indicate the presence of distinct transition routes determined by the metal's interaction with the substrate. It is revealed that the presence of an enzyme can influence the preferred reaction pathway. Additionally, based on these results, hypotheses are formulated regarding the mechanisms behind enzyme-assisted and catalyzed reactions. Importantly, these findings highlight the effectiveness of this global optimization technique in discovering the underlying physics behind complex, many-step reaction dynamics. It has been released with additional functionality to enable the analysis of multi-step reaction networks through the integration of rate constants. It is now possible to compute the underlying transition networks from the optimized pathways and evaluate the likelihood of each pathway for each step. In addition to computing inner transition state rates, the technique also calculates inner transition states and can visualize the energy landscape and the transition network using the network approximation. These results confirm that the transition states of the outermost atom are in line with the Arrhenius theory and that the inner transition states of the optimized pathways contain valuable information about the transition states of the barrier crossing events. In the future, the technique aims to determine the outermost atom's transition state for each step through optimization. The problem of translating natural language to SQL lies at the heart of various AI applications including data-to-text systems and database automation tools. Thanks to advancements in deep learning, cutting-edge data-to-text systems can effectively translate database queries into human language. Nevertheless, deep learning models still struggle to perform effectively when it comes to parsing database queries into their constituent parts, a skill required for generating queries from text. This paper presents key findings from a NIST language analysis challenge, focusing on parsing database queries into their underlying SQL code. Our work shows that a combination of pre-trained language models and auxiliary tasks leads to the best results among all the entries in the challenge. We developed a four-layered model that leverages a SQL-to-text dataset to translate SQL code back into query text, using this text to guide our analysis of the query using a SpaCy model, followed by another application of the pre-trained language model to extract crucial query information. Finally, we employ a rule-based system to convert the query information into the desired SQL code. Our approach won first place in the challenge, achieving a 64.5% accuracy on a benchmark dataset, surpassing the runner-up by a significant margin with a 16% improvement. We believe that successful task transfer between pre-trained models and auxiliary tasks offers valuable lessons for AI researchers and practitioners. We publicly share the code supporting this research at https://github.com/fhgh DayToSQL!.

Nevertheless, these models' complex interiors make it difficult to understand how they operate, a critical shortcoming for social science researchers relying on these systems. We strive to fill this knowledge gap through improved hate speech identification models that utilize multiple data sources, specifically targeting Spanish and Arabic content in social media platforms. By integrating human evaluation and path analysis, we aim to increase accuracy and uncover the underlying psychological drivers of hate speech, which could lead to the development of innovative prevention strategies. We believe that further joint efforts from social scientists and AI researchers are necessary to tackle the numerous AI-driven social challenges of the future. We explore the effects of different degree distributions on the dynamics of networks composed of binary neurons with excitatory connections. By utilizing various degree distributions and adjusting the mean connectivity of the network, we identify and analyze phase transitions between dynamic states, specifically focusing on synchronized states and for central patterns. Notably, the degree distribution significantly affects the boundary demarcating asynchronous states from synchronized states and can prevent the occurrence of boundary states in the asynchronous state. Moreover, the degree distribution impacts the type of synchronized patterns observed, including the number of possible solutions and their desynchronization points. Interestingly, the dynamics of the network can be predominantly influenced by a small portion of highly connected neurons, raising the possibility that biological networks may utilize degree distribution to achieve diverse functional capabilities. Overall, our results demonstrate that the dynamics of neural networks are profoundly affected by the details of the degree distribution within the network. Finally, our predictions are verified using experiments conducted on actual hardware.

Current automated repair methods face difficulties beyond their current capabilities, such as repairing flaws in parallel programming or addressing three distinct forms of fault that exist in object-oriented programming. The initial strategy typically used in automated repair is based on search-based methods, such as generating and evaluating potential program repairs through syntax-based modifications, with the goal of finding the most suitable repair through syntax-based comparisons. However, the effectiveness of this approach is constrained by a trilemma that restricts search efficiency, quality, and scope. To overcome this constraint, we have developed an innovative repair strategy that diverges from syntax-based repairs and instead makes repairs by introducing antagonistic code using natural language guidance, which was trained using adversarial training to repair a wide range of faults efficiently. Our Trilemma Overcoming Strategy trains fix templates for multiple repair tasks using adversarial training, natural language guidance, and a specific computer programming approach called GP. This strategy was put to the test on a variety of complex software bugs, such as parallel programming flaws and multiple errors in object-oriented programming. Our results indicate that the Trilemma Overcoming Strategy is more efficient and effective than traditional repair methods, and even outperforms our latest syntax-based repair approach, the CoFlfix, by a significant margin, repairing a large percentage of up to 71% of the assessed faults efficiently. However, our latest GP-based repair method still falls short of ideal results, motivating further advancements in automated repair techniques. The threat to public safety in large cities has become a major issue worldwide, and cities in Latin America are particularly affected, with homicide rates in the region being five times higher than rates in other parts of the world. In an effort to investigate the causes behind the high homicide rates in cities, we employed a statistical analysis approach using Markov chain techniques in a study of 93 cities in the Brazilian state of Goias during the period from 2002 to 2014. Our research discovered significant clusters of high homicide rates in both larger and smaller cities, with the exception of cities with very low or very high rates, and we found that cities with high rates in one time period were likely to maintain high rates in subsequent periods. These findings suggest that factors such as organised crime presence, poverty, and gun availability play a role in the variation of homicide rates between cities, and cities with high rates in one time period are likely to continue to struggle with high rates in the future. Additionally, we found that governments' efforts to address the issue through law enforcement have had limited success, and instead, addressing the underlying social and economic issues could be an important step towards improving public safety in cities. These outcomes were further validated through graphical analysis, and the importance of the findings is discussed through policy implications. Moreover, the methodology used in this study could be easily adapted to investigate other social indicators, and the technique of Markov chain analysis can provide valuable insights in policy-making and research. The research data is available in our repository at https://github.com/leomartins71/Goias-Homicides. In terms of the policy implications, the findings of this study could contribute to a more data-driven approach in decision-making, and the interaction between analytical researchers and public actors could facilitate this goal. Furthermore, the interaction between researchers from different fields and public officials could lead to a more collaborative and research-informed environment in public policy. These policy implications are confirmed through direct quotes from the participants in our study. The research participants are representatives of the state government of Goias, city mayors and councilors, non-governmental organizations and the academic community. A novel technique has been developed for creating motion-free 4D T2-weighted MRI images from the body. The approach combines a modified turbo spin echo sequence with a model-based approach to account for breathing motions. These modified images, which are not affected by respiratory movement, can be used for a range of applications such as tumor size assessment and radiation treatment planning in radiotherapy. To confirm its effectiveness, the technique was applied to 10 patients undergoing treatment for lung cancer and their images compared with conventional breath-hold images, revealing significant advancements in image quality, particularly in the reduction of diaphragmatic blurring. This resulted in the acquisition of high-quality body scans via free-breathing MRI in a shorter time than previously thought possible with 10-15 deep breaths instead of 18-22. This data validation supports the use of the new method as an improved standard of care for body scanning in radiotherapy treatment planning. Deep learning models have achieved great success across various tasks, but their large dimensions lead to excessive storage demands, prolonged inference times, and an increased carbon footprint. To address these issues, model compression techniques involve reducing a pre-trained, high-capacity model to a more efficient, yet equivalent format. Traditionally, model compression involves adjusting parameters such as weights, filters, or tensor dimensions. Notably, layer dimension compression can be quite challenging, especially for convolutional operators with local data flow patterns. To bridge this gap, we introduce InDistill, a unique method for compressing pre-trained models with data flow-based layers. By leveraging a set of predefined, narrow kernel filters, InDistill enables the compression of convolutional layers with spatial dimensions, such as those in ResNet50 and VGG16. Experimental evaluation of InDistill demonstrates its superiority over other model compression techniques, preserving a pre-trained model's accuracy while achieving substantial compression, including a notable 8.7x reduction in model size and 3.5x in inference time, all while maintaining inferences with <0.3% loss in accuracy for the analyzed datasets. Furthermore, InDistill is shown to outperform other methods in compressing a pre-trained, state-of-the-art model for natural language processing tasks such as text classification and sentence embedding. To facilitate model development, we provide a user-friendly, open-source Python library for InDistill, including the code and datasets used in our research. This repository can be accessed at https://github.com/moheyyesh/indistill. To visualily verify the model's performance, we created an interactive model compression demonstration at https://modelspress.github.io. This study investigates the effects of spatially dispersed grazing on the evolution of plant populations, incorporating both individual plant growth equations and Lotka Volterra predator-above-prey models using an agent-based approach. In both scenarios, our results reveal that intense grazing leads to the stabilization of systems previously prone to chaotic behavior. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that excessive grazing ultimately causes the complete disappearance of plant populations through a scenario previously uncaptured in theoretical models. Our proposed framework aims to enhance our understanding of ecological dynamics and design effective conservation strategies by simulating the interactions between grazing animals and the plant species they interact with. The framework is built upon a grid-based simulation environment where each plant or animal is represented as an entity with specific attributes and behaviors. The simulation environment is built in the GEMSE platform, utilizing a customized language to build simulations easily and efficiently. The simulations presented are completely parameter-free; instead, we used the behavior of plants and animals to distinguish between different parameter spaces, specifically resident and non-resident grazing spaces. Where $n$ represents the number of variables, $\tau$ the dimensionality scale of the problem, and $Z$ the value of the optimal objective function. This efficiency is attributed to several mechanisms that reduce the severity and frequency of very small entries as SBA operates. Consequently, the linear iteration limit $O(n)$ proves that, under uniform probability, very small entries occur infrequently, alleviating the aporetic nature of SBA. Where $m$ represents the number of constraints. This performance guarantee contrasts with previous iterations of APS, which experienced an exponential, $O(2^m)$ efficiency loss. At present, no system exists to support task-adaptable neural networks that can be easily understood by non-experts. We aim to create a compact, adaptable program that can be translated from a task-based graph neural network model by utilizing a formal translation framework. A new translator has been developed, based on a formal translation framework, which allows for an efficient and automatic translation process. Experimental results demonstrate superior parameter optimization methods to conventional hyperparameter optimization techniques. Furthermore, the flexibility of our translator enables the creation of complex graph neural networks as well as other deep learning models not covered by existing tools. We showcase its capabilities in areas like program synthesis and semantic analysis. Overall, our system presents a novel approach to task-adaptable neural networks. We demonstrate its effectiveness in optimizing the parameters of a GNN program by achieving a top-1 accuracy of 97.85% in graph classification. Additionally, our system allows for the program size to be reduced without compromising accuracy. Such flexibility and efficiency could potentially lead to new avenues in the research domain. The peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central cluster core. To explore its structural properties, we studied the morphological features of the system at multiple scales, using X-ray data in the core and outer regions, as well as the large-scale environment observed from radio data. We found contrasting findings with respect to the core and the surrounding areas: while the core exhibits no notable substructures that could be responsible for the radio signal, the large-scale environment shows clear signs of past mergers, including a disturbed morphology visible in X-ray data and a head-tail galaxy presence, which correlates with the halogenated radio signal. These results indicate that the large-scale system far exceeds the core-scale merger activity by an order of magnitude, implying a primary source of the halo emission is not the core merger but rather the past mergers in the large-scale environment. Our study underlines the significance of examining the surrounding large-scale environment to understand the origin of radio haloes in galaxy clusters. Additionally, it highlights the potential of radio data in mapping the environment's morphology, a technique that proved more sensitive to the surrounding large-scale features than X-ray data. Finally, it highlights the unique properties of RXCJ0232.2-4420, serving as a representative of relaxed core but disturbed large-scale environment, and also as an ideal system to further study rare occurrences of radio haloes in galaxy clusters. We recommend that future studies focus on the large-scale environment of galaxy clusters using radio data, enhancing our comprehension of the environment's morphology, and also helping to identify the origins of radio haloes and relics. PINN's accuracy can be compromised due to spectral bias, a phenomenon where neural networks prefer low-frequency solutions over complex ones. This issue is particularly pronounced when PINNs are used to solve PDEs with intricate details. Although training multiple iterations can mitigate the problem, each simulation is expensive and time-consuming. This paper explores the potential of using the momentum term in the gradient descent optimizer to reduce spectral bias. The introduction of momentum leads to a more smooth and continuous weight space, allowing the network to capture a wider range of frequencies. Our experiments demonstrate that utilizing momentum can significantly improve the performance of PINNs for complex tasks, such as solving the Sod problem and approximating solutions for Riemann problems at multiple interfaces. By leveraging momentum, PINNs are able to reproduce accurate solutions while requiring fewer simulations, consistent with theoretical expectations. Additionally, our findings reveal that optimizing towards intermediate frequencies can facilitate faster convergence. Ultimately, this research validates the efficacy of momentum as a complementary approach to addressing spectral bias in PINNs. The proposed method has significant implications for optimizing PINNs, enabling them to solve a broader range of difficult problems more efficiently. Importantly, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the impact of spectral bias, the behavior of momentum in optimizing algorithms, and the factors influencing the choice of regularization methods, all of which are crucial considerations for PINN design. These insights can be easily extended to other deep learning architectures beyond PINNs, including other physics-informed networks such as those employing loss functions for volume-to-surface optimization. Moreover, our research demonstrates that bias-variance tradeoffs are inherent to neural network optimization, offering a valuable foundation for the future design of deep learning algorithms. To address this challenge, we propose a model-driven hierarchical reinforcement learning framework, wherein a high-level agent delegates tasks to lower-level agents, leveraging pre-defined rules. Despite its potential, implementing this concept proves complicated in practice. To tackle this issue, we propose an integrated methodology that synthesizes rule extraction, meta-learning, and multi-level reinforcement learning. Our system employs inductive logic programming to extract task-specific rules from the observations of a learner, which is treated as an agent. Additionally, we define a set of general rules encompassing possible actions for each task and establish a method for transferring extracted rules to novel tasks, thus facilitating the creation of a comprehensive library of reusable rules. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in creating a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework with a set of adaptable rules. Our results also show that the extracted rules can successfully encode those underlying to human intelligence, revealing our methodology as a means for model-driven reinforcement learning research and development. We have thoroughly evaluated the algorithmic efficiency of our proposed framework, complete with step-by-step implementation guidance. Our findings confirm that our methodology is capable of generating task-specific and general rules with high accuracy, thus supporting its practical application. Additionally, we have analyzed the expert knowledge required for its implementation, revealing that the complexity of the data impacts the difficulty of the knowledge acquisition task. Our experience has also underscored the importance of the initial conditions, highlighting the necessity of an efficient learner for successful knowledge extraction. To facilitate the reproduction of our work, we have made available the implementation code, data, and experimental results. Our study has successfully addressed the challenge of the reinvestment problem, paving the way for model-driven reinforcement learning research and development. This constraint is represented by the logarithm of the trace norm, and its violation indicates the existence of non-classical effects. Researchers have employed various tools, such as additivity, to analyze this limit and its implications. A particular challenge arises from the possibility of inducing this limit incompatibility through the use of quantum channels. Our study demonstrates that there exists a specific quantum channel capable of transforming an arbitrary input state into a compressed form that cannot be further compressed due to the violation of the quantum compression limit. This finding is remarkable as the lower bound of the logarithm of the trace norm remains unattainable, and it becomes evident that the quantum compression limit is a necessary condition for its logarithmic counterpart. By exploring this issue further, we investigate whether this limit incompatibility can be induced in an optically accessible manner. Our analysis reveals that, despite the possibility of achieving it in the context of odd-dimensional systems, it remains unachievable in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional systems. A particular quantum channel, specifically a four-polarization mode bosonic mode-squeezed transformer, when used in a two-dimensional system, serves as the critical component in inducing the quantum compression limit incompatibility. This finding presents the quantum compression limit incompatibility as a phenomenon confined to higher dimensions, and it underscores the difficulty of experimentally inducing it using linear optics. Ultimately, it challenges the experimental community to achieve and analyze the effects of this non-classical phenomenon. Our study has also led to the identification of incompressible states with specific entropy bounds that preserve the impossibility of further compression. Specifically, it has allowed us to derive a lower entropy bound with the same logarithmic scale as the trace norm, and confirm its implementation in systems comprising four and five photons, and in dimensions ranging from three to twenty-three. Moreover, it has allowed us to derive an alternative compression limit as a multi-dimensional phenomenon and to challenge the community to achieve and analyze the effects of this non-classical phenomenon. The CRESST experiment is one of the leading projects for dark matter research based on cryogenic silicon and diamond targets. By examining the heat signals from these targets and the ionization signals from associated light particles, the experiment can investigate both scalar and vector interactions of dark matter. By utilizing multiple target materials with varying densities and atomic numbers, the experiment can differentiate between interactions that depend on mass versus those that are independent of mass. This paper presents an innovative solution to the blind image restoration problem. Typically addressed by generating numerous deconvolution pairs to create a "dictionary" of point spreads functions, our approach instead relies on a mixture of Gaussian kernels. The Gaussian kernel set can be limitless, yet training-based methods exploit these sets' limitations to fall short in real-world applications. In contrast, our framework leverages the inherent properties of these distributions to extract low-quality sensor images, which are then utilized as prior knowledge in a variational Bayesian deconvolution framework. Diverging from conventional dictionary-based methods, our algorithm generates priors tailored to each specific image without requiring extensive training, while also accommodating heterogeneous sensor phenomena. Through comprehensive tests on synthetic and real-world datasets, our methodology consistently demonstrates superior performance over standard dictionary-based methods and state-of-the-art blind image restoration techniques. Our findings further demonstrate that accurate low-quality image prior generation is crucial for achieving optimal restoration results. Additionally, we propose a novel Gaussian kernel selection method to complement our framework, providing a self-sufficient solution for blind image restoration that does not rely on trainability. The popular "Lights Out" game has an expanded version with n x n lights where players take turns resolving systems of linear equations simultaneously. This game's solutions were previously understood to result in a TMS-like tree structure with depth n - 1, and a known strategy allowed players to win in n - 2 steps under optimal conditions. However, a fundamental paradox arose when considering optimal player moves indicating a likely loss in n - 2 steps. This study presents the first explicit description of a strategy allowing players to win in n - 2 steps and demonstrates the existence of "maximum clicks" scenarios where both players win or lose in the same step regardless of additional conditions. This contrasts with the original game's properties as well as previous studies on related games. An investigation into these "maximum clicks" scenarios revealed they are identifiable using a particular set of conditions. This inquiry aims to reframe the original win condition, asking if there are any situations where a player can win in n - 2 steps by executing any maximum clicks scenario. If this condition holds true for all two-player scenarios, it would imply the existence of a new, distinct winning strategy. To address this, a classification system was created to organize various maximum clicks scenarios according to unique characteristics. Utilizing this framework, a theoretical "first move" condition was established for winning scenarios, and a corresponding set of rules that could lead to a universal winning strategy was proposed. A practical demonstration of this condition revealed that it is generally achievable in some specific cases. If the condition holds true for all possible "maximum clicks" scenarios, it would mark a significant breakthrough in this area of study. An accompanying conjecture suggests the existence of a direct relationship between a player's ability to execute a "first move" and their potential to win in n - 2 steps. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of "maximum clicks" scenarios while proposing novel ideas for reframe the original win condition and explore the existence of a universal winning strategy. The research also raises essential questions for future inquiry. The first part of this thesis focuses on making the "Lights Out" game solvable under any "maximum clicks" condition, and the second half delves into its broader implications. The goal is to identify conditions that can lead to a winning strategy for "maximum clicks" scenarios, with an accompanying list of open problems that still persist in the field. In particular, this thesis aims to make the "Lights Out" game solvable under any "maximum clicks" condition for the first time and proposes a practical solution in the process

To address these limitations, we propose an innovative, interactive review-based product recommendation model called SIFN. This model integrates a review encoder and a product recommender through a novel, iterative back-propagation process, known as Cyber-Loop, to iteratively refine review representations and product embeddings until convergence. Experimental results on three public real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of SIFN over 25 state-of-the-art baselines across four evaluation metrics. Notably, the model outperforms a strong ablation variant of itself, known as Fine-tuned SIFN, which is further supported by in-depth analysis. These findings highlight the importance of interactive learning, multi-grade attention, and the consideration of sentiment levels in review-based product recommendation. In the context of general lambda deformations, we identify a group of states, referred to as connectable branes, that are capable of being embedded across separate factors of the metric. The key example in this analysis involves kappa deformations, which derive their origin from the type of action taken, namely Yang--Mills or super Yang--Mills. Two prominent branes are investigated within this study: those related to coadjoint replications and the soliton found in the replica of the SU(2) group. Solitons of Yang--Mills action exhibit unaltered internal metrics but undergo transformations in their two-form metrics when considering super Yang--Mills action. Additionally, branes associated with coadjoint replications undergo alterations in both their internal metrics. Various connectable brane combinations are presented, combining both coadjoint replications and the SU(2) soliton. These composite brane configurations are shown to be equivalent to those found in undressed lambda deformations, both in terms of metric and two-form distortion. Combining however the deformation of the soliton with itself results in distortion not only of the brane but also its internal structures. Combining the deformation of the soliton with Yang--Mills configurations however reveals a distinct scenario in which soliton internal structures are protected from such distortion. Using an existing physical interpretation of lambda deformations, an explicit description is given of how these branes can be viewed as particles in deformed spaces whose deforming forces derive from group actions. Furthermore, it is shown that these branes are also realizations of particles in standard Minkowski space but now subject to non-standard, group-mediated interactions. Lastly, some preliminary thoughts are given regarding connectable brane combinations based on reps with lower symmetry than SU(2), namely reps with rank = 1 and U(1) groups. It has been demonstrated that these branes are distinct from lambda deformations generated from reps with rank = 2 and SU(2), nor are they equivalent to lambda deformations generated from reps with rank = 1 and their respective groups, although they can be viewed as generalized versions thereof. Notably, it is also shown that these branes are distinct from one another in both their internal one-forms. Combining these two scenarios therefore results in a distinct composite brane configuration which is transcriptionally and transcriptionally equivalent to those found in undressed lambda deformations, both in terms of metric and two-form distortion. State-of-the-art performance in relation extraction is often achieved using pre-trained language models (LMs). However, these models have been observed to perform poorly when dealing with rare or unseen relations in testing phase. This study demonstrates that LM's ability to capture relation information can also be utilized for link prediction in Knowledge Graphs (KGs), which in turn enables improved relation extraction results. By leveraging a broad collection of KG data sets, it has been observed that the constraints imposed by a KG for predicting links of a specific subject can be effectively employed as a filter to eliminate incorrect relation sentences. This technique is exemplified through experiments conducted on General Conceptual Embedding (GCE) and Struct2Vec models, showing that the application of relation extraction and KG link prediction are interdependent and complementary tasks, resulting in enhanced overall performance. Notably, it has been found that the optimal hyper-parameter configuration for KG link prediction also positively impacts the final relation extraction results. Consequently, it is proposed that the integration of LM-based relation extraction with KG link prediction, via a shared resource, forms an effective joint task to further improve overall performance in relation extraction from scarce data. The research suggests that the future direction for enhancing LM-based relation extraction lies in developing advanced multi-task frameworks that integrate various NLP and Information Retrieval tasks, including KG link prediction, to address the data scarcity in relation extraction. This proposed idea has been exemplified through an experimental demonstration showing the practical implications of our research on the development of a semi-automatic relation extraction tool from scarce text resources. Based on the research conducted, it is recommended that the optimization of LM parameters for KG link prediction also improves final relation extraction performance, thereby offering a time-saving alternative to manual relation verification process, at least for rare relations. Finally, the research is positioned to contribute to the development of a new multi-task framework for information retrieval applications with scarce data, as well as other related tasks supported by a broad collection of KG data sets. The experimental results from 13 different data sets show that the proposed idea has successfully improved performance over existing state-of-the-art relation extraction methods by at least 8% in F1 measure. In multi-agent learning systems, ensuring stable cooperation is a significant concern when interacting with uncertain or unpredictable partners. We propose a principle of transfer empowerment as a motivational mechanism to address this issue. Transfer empowerment captures the idea that an agent's capabilities and skills should influence its motivation to engage in tasks, which in turn affects its interactive behavior with other agents. By enhancing an agent's perceived abilities through training, transfer empowerment leads to an internal motivation for self-improvement in tasks lacking substantial rewards, thereby empowering it to adapt to more challenging tasks in the future. We develop transfer empowerment as a variational autoencoder-based framework and apply it to the problem of repeatedly playing a categorization task against unpredictable partners. Experimental results show that our approach, dubbed RE-responder, achieves stable and consistent cooperation with random partners beyond its initial training scope, surpassing existing methods built upon adaptation or intrinsic reward systems. Overall, the underlying theory of transfer empowerment highlights the significance of distinguishing an agent's skills from its controllable actions and provides a framework for regulating an agent's self-improvement efforts based on its perceived abilities. The provided codes enable easy replication of our experiments, which also demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in various practical scenarios, as documented in our accompanying website. A pre-trained model and player can be directly downloaded from the given links. Analysis of the approach also identifies potential drawbacks similar to existing intrinsic reward systems, specifically issues of unexplored game states, inflated expectations, and race of exploration versus exploitation, which are discussed along with strategies to mitigate these side effects. Ultimately, the theoretical foundation of transfer empowerment highlights the importance of transferring learned skills to addressing the stable cooperation problem, particularly by differentiating skills from actions and assessing an agent's abilities to regulate motivation. The approach of transfer empowerment specifically influences an agent's motivation to respond to partner behaviors by emphasizing the development of its skills and abilities for enhanced cooperation, as demonstrated in our experiments with the RE-responder method. A key finding of our research reveals that many existing intrinsic reward systems lack a systematic way to distinguish an agent's skills from its controllable actions, which is critical for achieving transfer of skills and enhancing cooperation with unpredictable partners, as achieved by the RE-responder method. While our approach shares some similarities with intrinsic reward systems in the transfer of learned experiences, we distinctly regulate motivation by emphasizing the development of an agent's skills and abilities beyond its initial training scope, thereby differentiating the concept of transfer empowerment from existing intrinsic reward systems. The aim is to develop an automatic system for linking image components to reference models, independent of the detector's location. We create an innovative technique called LoFTR, combining self-attention mechanisms, for matching local image features to reference models without relying on a detector. We conduct experiments using the reference-based local feature matching dataset, which contains distinct benchmarks. Our analysis using both a mobile device and NVIDIA GPU demonstrates that LoFTR performs efficiently in terms of both speed and memory usage. The precise determination of the absolute solar vector magnetic field (VSFM) is crucial for understanding the dynamics of magnetic field observations. Since the solar photosphere is opaque to visible radiation, we must use indirect methods like the least-squares deconvolution and minimum distance methods to infer the VSFM from spectro-polarimetric observations. These techniques are, however, susceptible to bias from various sources, which can greatly impact the accuracy and reliability of the VSFM. This study aims to identify the causes of this bias, utilizing a simulated dataset, and proposes a new approach to mitigate its effects. Specifically, we demonstrate that employing the minimum distance technique with a large regularization parameter can significantly alleviate bias in a controlled simulation. Moreover, we show that using the correlation matrix instead of a diagonal matrix in the least-squares deconvolution method bias it towards the original polarimeter and affects the symmetry of the magnetic field maps. By removing the mean and scaling the residuals using the standard deviation, we can minimize the bias from small-scale noise and ensure the accuracy of the VSFM. This technique also has the added benefit of reducing noise in regions where the magnetic field is zero. Our findings have important implications for the development of inversion codes, which we hope will inspire further work to tackle this bias. This research has significant potential to enhance our understanding of the solar magnetic field dynamics. Moreover, we intend to extend this study in future research to tackle bias in other astrophysical sources. This research explores a real-world scenario where consumers as well as energy providers participate in a global energy market. To mitigate voltage problems, distribution system operators enforce load reduction during emergency situations. The study focuses on a strategy adopted by distribution systems to impose random load charges on consumers in real-time, aiming to stimulate users' proactive management of their energy consumption. The proposed framework consists of two key parts: forecasting energy usage patterns and distributing real-time load charges. The first component develops a predictive model for determining consumers' energy usage schedules. The second part employs a collective game theory approach to calculate optimal and coordinated real-time load charges for all participants, including both consumers and energy providers. The effectiveness of the proposed model is validated through a multi-period linear programming approach. The study also incorporates real-world constraints such as battery capacity, energy storage efficiency, and energy availability into the modeling process. The outcomes of the study highlight the trade-offs between consumers' energy usage schedules and real-time load charges, illustrating the ability of collective game theory to produce a Pareto-optimal solution effectively and efficiently. The study also shows that compliance with real-time load charges has a positive impact on achieving optimal energy usage schedules. The study further examines how various factors, such as consumer and provider participation, influencing the choice of solution type and impact of non-participation in real-time load charging. The study also validates the feasibility of the proposed model using actual data from the ISO New England energy market. The study's outcomes demonstrate its practical applicability to real-world scenarios, encompassing diverse energy usage patterns, including residential, commercial, and industrial sectors. The study's critical takeaway is that collective game theory offers an efficient approach to developing and implementing independent demand control strategies that take into account the interconnected needs of both consumers and energy providers. Compressing large deep neural networks by reducing their size while retaining their predictive abilities has become a crucial challenge in today's AI era. Existing studies mainly focused on compressing already-trained models based on their behavior or parameters, but they do not account for the data they'll be using after compression. In our study, we tackle this issue by proposing a novel framework called POMCom, which views model compression as a state estimation problem where the compressor has limited information about the input data. POMCom is based on two key concepts: 1) a compression controller that makes informed decisions based on observed model outputs, and 2) a Bayes-optimal compression strategy that maximizes predictive accuracy by treating compression as a state estimation problem. Our results show that POMCom can be applied across various compression methods to significantly improve the accuracy of compressed models by obtaining the optimal compression strategy through the Bayes-optimal state estimator. Notably, POMCom represents a breakthrough since it requires no training, unsupervised and does not rely on sample data. It is especially useful for dynamic environments where there may not be enough data to train a model from scratch. Additionally, POMCom offers a range of theoretical benefits, including the ability to identify the optimal compression strategy under perfect conditions, and its ability to adapt to real-world scenarios with imperfect data. Our study used POMCom to improve the accuracy of compressed models in image classification tasks by up to 4.88% and reduced the size of these models by up to 40.2% in terms of computation complexity. POMCom has also outperformed state-of-the-art model compression methods in various applications such as language modeling and sequence classification. POMCom source code can be found at https://github.com/harveyw/POCOM. Yet, the increased computational complexity stemming from a lack of frequency spectrum utilization and robustness to phase errors in traditional non-coherent CPM detection methods has been a notable shortcoming. Research has shown that this complexity can be substantial enough to surpass the advantages offered by increased processing gains in certain scenarios. In such cases, deeper unfolding of the traditional non-coherent CPM detection structure can lead to a significant reduction in processing complexity, surpassing that of other notable modulation schemes such as Gaussian minimum shift keying (GMSK). The following work involves the examination of three delay reduction techniques, which successfully integrate the traditional non-coherent CPM detection methods while achieving considerable delay reduction. The proposed solutions are evaluated based on their average detection error ratios and average processing times via Monte Carlo simulations, utilizing a 128 MSPS GMSK transmitter, for a range of CPM modulation types. A novel optimization algorithm called VACRank is introduced to enhance reward learning speed with human-involvement via video feedback. VACRank leverages Hierarchical Clustering of State-Action Policies to streamline the reward shaping process, offering accelerated reward learning and increased reliability. Human-provided score distributions inform the clustering of similar State-Action Policies, narrowing the search space for sub-optimal reward iterations. Additionally, VACRank's clustering framework allows the integration of existing expert policies, enhancing optimization robustness and resilience to sub-optimal trajectories. We validate VACRank's performance on a dataset of ranked downlink wireless data-path videos and evaluate its efficacy in environment simulation. Moreover, we showcase VACRank's ability to precisely replicate human scoring metrics across various domains, establishing its generalizability to new, unseen environments. Finally, we validate VACRank's capability to achieve optimal rankings in the absence of human supervision, leveraging expert policies and the structure of the clustering framework to facilitate automatic optimization. Results demonstrate VACRank's superiority over conventional optimization algorithms, achieving higher accuracy and reliability with the same amount of human data. Importantly, VACRank's clustering framework allows the automatic creation of dense ranking heatmaps, facilitating human data-efficient recovery, even in high-dimensional environments. Overall, VACRank provides a scalable, human-assisted solution for time-Effective reward learning, even in complex multi-step environments. The proposed algorithm achieves generalizability, reliability, and high-dimensional scalability, effectively addressing the reward learning challenge. To establish trust in decision-making aid algorithms, their transparency must be increased.  Understanding a transparent algorithm requires less effort when its logic is straightforward and understandable in plain terms, whereas intricate algorithms with many components are more difficult to grasp for humans.  We create a new scoring system called CIA, or Cognitive Interpretability Assessment, which gauges a learning-based algorithm's clarity using human cognitive capabilities as a reference point.  We analyze multiple algorithms that perform black-box learning, such as decision tree, random forest, and gradient boosting, along with white-box algorithms including neural networks and Gaussian processes.  By testing various patterns of artificial data, we evaluate how well humans can predict an algorithm's decisions, taking into consideration the algorithm's explainability based on its rule sets, its learned parameters, and its logic in plain terms.  Our results demonstrate that there's a direct link between an algorithm's learnability and its ability to be understood by humans, establishing that learnability is not solely determined by an algorithm's complexity or its similarity to simple models.  Furthermore, we discovered a direct link between an algorithm's interpretability and its ability to handle difficult problems, as well as its resistance to instability in its parameters and training processes, suggesting that CIA is an effective measure for assessing a learning-based algorithm's transparency.  We intend to develop additional tools and databases that can measure an algorithm's CIA in more detail.  Additionally, the results of this study offer suggestions for improving an algorithm's transparency, suggesting that incorporating diverse views of data can enhance its logic in plain terms and its ability to handle difficult problems, while regular checks on its parameters and processes can strengthen its stability, as these factors are key determinants of an algorithm's transparency, as measured by CIA.  Ultimately, the study suggests that combining multiple factors must be taken into account when assessing an algorithm's transparency, as suggested by the scoring system for CIA.  As such, the proposed scoring system for interpreting algorithms is valuable for learning-based algorithms in that it provides a direct link between human understanding and algorithmic transparency, as well as a clear set of criteria for evaluating and improving an algorithm's transparency, as determined by CIA.  Importantly, the study provides valuable insights into the nature of transparency, as understood by humans, suggesting that it is not solely determined by an algorithm's complexity or its consistency in its decisions, as these factors may not necessarily contribute to an algorithm's transparency, as determined by CIA. Quantum physics contradicts classical probability in how it treats state information, especially with the concept of state non determinism. This unique treatment generates inherent inconsistencies in inferring probabilities within quantum frameworks. For instance, the application of Bayes' Theorem in updating probability distributions is, in fact, infeasible when state non determinism prevails. Consequently, the feasibility of using quantum extensions of Bayes' Theorem, such as the quantum Bayes' Theorem of Uhlmann and Fuchs, raises crucial implications for scientific inquiry in fields like quantum physics, where evidence is interpreted through indirect means such as quantum-level predictions. When applied consistently, the quantum Bayes' Theorem of Uhlmann and Fuchs enables accurate prediction validation for both classical and quantum phenomena. Furthermore, the use of this theorem highlights the necessity of validating non-deterministic quantum predictions by observing positive correlations among multiple events, an insight also applicable in validating non-deterministic classical predictions. Interestingly, when applied to quantum-level predictions, the application of quantum Bayes' Theorem reveals the validity of commonly accepted quantum-level predictions regarding spin measurements. Finally, the feasibility of using quantum Bayes' Theorem raises significant epistemological questions regarding the nature and limitations of indirect scientific evidence, as well as the understanding of causation, particularly in fields like quantum physics. Discussion is also extended to these topics. Physical keyless authentication protocols provide security without encryption keys by verifying the identities of participants in physical systems. We developed a unified framework to quantify the disturbance a legitimate user can introduce into an adversary's measurement system, thereby preventing the adversary from engaging in covert attacks. Our results apply to a wide range of keyless authentication protocols, and are demonstrated using two well-known protocols, the quantum two-stage authentication protocol and the quantum dual-use protocol, all within the context of an additive white Gaussian noise channel. Our findings also highlight potential security risks that arise from disrupting these keyless authentication protocols. Additionally, we established a lower bound on the disturbance that can be introduced by authenticating sources, and showed that this bound improves as the authentication source sends more messages, and that it is possible for an untrusty verifier to always verify or discard the authenticating source's messages without introducing any disturbance in the worst case scenario. Nevertheless, it is still possible for authenticating sources to guarantee their authenticity and impose disturbance on potential adversaries, even in the scenario where the verifiers' responses are unknown to the adversaries. Moreover, we found that the channel capacity for transmitting disturbance, which is the maximum rate of authenticating messages that can still introduce disturbance to an adversary, is defined by the cross-entropies of the authenticating source and the adversary's measurement mixtures, and that it is possible for authenticating sources to reach this channel capacity by sending mixed states, which is particularly beneficial in the scenario where the authenticating source and the adversary have limited control over each other. Lastly, we demonstrated the applicability of these key findings to the quantum dual-use protocol using an example. In summary, these conclusions provide the groundwork for identifying the essential components of a successful keyless authentication protocol, which we hope to expand upon in our future research. Quantitative analysis of these key findings may reveal additional insights that can refine the design of keyless authentication protocols, which may ultimately contribute to the creation of secure communication systems, as well as stimulate breakthroughs in cryptographic techniques that leverage disturbances to ensure security without encryption keys. One such breakthrough could potentially involve the development of secure keyless dual-use protocols that utilize disturbances to carry out both authentication and covert attacks, thereby achieving security without encryption keys. Numerical examples of these key findings that apply to additive white Gaussian noise channels provide a clear understanding of the trade-offs between disturbance and authentication performance for keyless authentication protocols, and highlight potential security risks, including the possibility of launching covert attacks and disrupting authenticating sources. Nevertheless, the equilibrium might be inaccessible due to the presence of local minima in parameter spaces encountered by neural network-based agents. Employing Fixed Point Networks, trained on a sequence of fixed-point iterations, enables the avoidance of such local minima and facilitates the direct targeting of the equilibrium, thereby prompting the development of FPNet, a novel algorithm. FPNet achieves this by having the policy network realize its own fixed-point iterations as a distinct task. Through extensive evaluation, FPNet exhibits superior capacity in playing finite, mixed-strategy games, particularly those encompassing Repeated Prisoner's Dilemma and Rock-Paper-Scissors. Notably, FPNet outperforms cutting-edge recent approaches while achieving more stable results. Moreover, FPNet demonstrates novel understanding of cooperative and competitive game behaviors. For instance, FPNet demonstrates Rock-Paper-Scissors equilibrium in the Rock-Paper-Scissors game. This study explores ways to assess the influence of one random variable on another using information theory and entropy. A significant finding was that conditional entropy can effectively measure the maximum possible impact of one variable on another, and this relationship holds under all possible conditions. Additionally, we have expanded existing theories to include cases involving multiple variables and high-dimensional information structures. Our analysis under non-ignorant conditions reveals that conditional entropy and mutual information can both influence this influence, while under completely random and unrelated scenarios, these effects can be quantified as specific dimensions or scales. Our examination of real-world data also demonstrates the applicability of this influence measure to complex information patterns. Lastly, we have discussed some potential practical uses and limitations of this influence measure. This work is an advancement in the field of information theory, particularly in the areas of causality and high-dimensional information structures. A key aspect of this investigation is that it relies on entropy-based measures rather than more complex probability distributions, making it a distinctive contribution in this area.

A document summary is a condensed version of a longer text, typically used to give a brief overview. Most current summary generation techniques are designed to handle only limited languages and face numerous challenges when applied to longer texts. To overcome these issues, a novel Graph Attention Enhanced summarization model (GAE-ISumm) is suggested for Indian languages, which operates independently without human oversight. This model leverages unique properties from each sentence in a document, similar to human readers, to produce a summary based on the document's underlying graph structure. The GAE-ISumm model utilizes Transformer-based graph structures and incorporates an attention-based sentence selector, making it an efficient and innovative method. The model's effectiveness was evaluated using datasets in three Indian languages - Hindi, Gujarati, and Sanskrit - and the results demonstrate that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in summary quality. The research presents GAE-ISumm as the first self-supervised summarization model for Indian languages and introduces Sanskrit summarization, a previously unexplored area. The model's source code is publicly available, contributing to the development of more sophisticated Indian language NLP models. Experimental results indicate that GAE-ISumm produces summaries of higher quality compared to existing state-of-the-art models in terms of coherence, specifically by 2.2, having similar fluency, and also shows an improvement of 4.0 in coherence while maintaining similar fluency compared to fine-tuning models. The model's summary sample quality is comparable to those generated by professional writers in terms of fluency and coherence. The research presents a comprehensive assessment of the model's performance, providing valuable automated evaluation of summary quality. The assessment outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in terms of coherence, and also matches the summary quality of more advanced fine-tuned models in terms of fluency. Therefore, the model shows significant progress in induced graph structures. Additionally, the model's performance indicates that (i) sentence similarity does not directly translate to summary quality, (ii) induced graph structures can lead to improved summary quality, and (iii) the Coherence Score is a more reliable metric compared to average sentence similarity for assessing summary quality in induced graph structures. To further develop the model, the researchers plan to (i) incorporate diverse human-annotated graph structures, (ii) utilize additional graph structure features, (iii) improve the model's ability to leverage these graph structure features, (iv) incorporate additional sentence-level attributes, and (v) incorporate human-annotated summary labels for more effective training. High-bit-rate communications signal waveforms can be efficiently encoded using gray-coded modulation, significantly reducing the data transmission rate by at least one bit. However, the resulting increased idle time due to the start-of-symbol pattern necessitates a pattern occurrence frequency map, which incites a new problem. Most existing solutions either compromise communication rate or start-of-symbol pattern repetition. To address this, an approach called learning value quantization for gray-coded encoding has been developed. A neural network is employed to determine the start-of-symbol pattern patternicity matrix, which identifies the frequency of each pattern and assigns a value to each occurrence. To optimize the matrix, a loss function is defined as the sum of average values of all patterns and idle time due to the start-of-symbol pattern patternicity matrix, and a gradient-based algorithm calculates the optimal matrix that minimizes the average value, thereby reducing idle time. Results show that this new approach can achieve a 50% reduction in the number of value bits with negligible performance loss and at least a 93% reduction in idle time with only a 1-bit increase in the number of value bits, both measured relative to standard gray-coded encoding. These results also show that the neural network has the potential for be adapted across different start-of-symbol pattern distributions. Furthermore, the neural network-based solution can easily be integrated with existing communication systems with minimal design alterations. It's also notable that the neural network-based solution requires significantly fewer training steps than classical optimization methods to achieve optimized performance. Crowdsourced labeling, commonly used for classifying diverse real-world data sets, has seen significant growth along with the development of Machine Learning. Although popular, crowdsourcing comes with several issues that necessitate careful consideration. Not only does labeling data require significant time, but crowdworkers also frequently provide inconsistent labels for the same data. This research investigates a specific data set: "5-Scores," which consists of five-class data collected through crowdsourcing with enhanced reliability measures. Each labeled 5-Score includes a confidence score and the majority vote of crowdworkers. While the majority vote reflects the dataset's class outcome, the included confidence scores facilitate predicting labeling uncertainty. In consequence, only data points with high confidence scores are considered authentic, while those with lower confidence scores are viewed as noisy. As a result, noisy data points can cause inaccuracies in the resulting model. To address this, this study developed two methods to identify and exclude noisy data points based on entropy-based metrics. The research also compared and evaluated various techniques for authentic data set reconstruction, including different training methods for constructing authentic data set models, and discovered that a specific approach, "hard voting," yielded superior results. The research also discovered that modifying the distribution of a model's classes can substantially impact its accuracy, and that this can be accomplished by adding a entropy-based regularizer to a model. When this modified model is trained with both authentic and noisy data, the resulting model can accurately classify both. Notably, while the research did not address the underlying cause of labeling uncertainty, it did successfully create a model that accurately classifies data despite the presence of noisy data points. The research also uncovered significant and unexpected patterns within the data distribution, specifically regarding the relationship between the classes 'dog' and 'cat,' as well as a significant spike in the 'other' class at data point 3577. The research concludes by highlighting its key findings and suggesting several potential areas of future investigation. The resulting dataset, 'human_softmax_5scores,' has been made publicly available on GitHub, and is intended for use as a reference data set for researchers and educators. The research has several significant implications, specifically regarding the value of entropy-based metrics in labeling data, the importance of considering confidence scores when building crowdsourced datasets, and the effectiveness of hard voting in building models from crowdsourced data. The research has also demonstrated that a model can accurately classify data even when provided with noisy data points. In a contest with information concealment, individual contestants attempt to win by submitting a value, and only one gains the prize, typically awarded based on the contestant's submitted value. This system has been shown to be effective in keeping costs private during negotiations. When dealing with a large number of contestants, the game becomes significantly more complicated as each contestant must assess the possible submissions of all participants. This complex nature is reduced in the standard contest model, as players generally only consider the strategies of their immediate rivals. However, when private and potentially limitless information is involved, determining an optimal policy becomes extremely challenging, if not impossible, especially in environments with many contestants. This complexity is even greater when considering the strategies of multiple opponents. However, for a unique class of private contests where winners are chosen within a specified range, the researchers have established a mathematical framework for finding policies that make strategic sense, showing that such policies can be found more easily and even exactly in some special cases of private contests. This framework builds on a concept called'maximally intertwined states' first introduced by Friesen et al. for a separate type of private contest. By applying novel ideas rooted in graph theory, the researchers have precisely characterized the policies that make strategic sense in these special cases. Consequently, the study reveals that such policies can be found more easily in these special cases of private contests than in general private contests where the graph-theoretic analysis becomes increasingly difficult as the number of participants grows. Despite this, the study suggests that determining an optimal policy in these special cases remains a computationally feasible problem, if not an impossible one, for a large number of participants. In contrast, the study suggests that determining an optimal policy in general private contests remains a highly infeasible problem, if not an impossible one, for any special case where the graph of interconnected participants becomes complex, even with the aid of a very fast computer. For the most part, conversations in everyday life are smooth and happen at a steady pace, however, when interacting with speech assistants, conversations are frequently interrupted by interruptions, specifically, speech interruptions. Current research methods primarily use speech signal analysis combined with machine learning to identify and categorize speech interruptions. This paper suggests an alternative approach that focuses specifically on measuring the discrepancies in conversational tempo, governed by the synchronization distance. The proposed method relies on a deep learning model to automatically identify speech interruptions solely from the acoustic features of speech interactions, eliminating the need for manual annotation. The dataset employed in this research consists of conversational speech collected from volunteers through the Amazon Mechanical Turk platform, accompanied by corresponding audio recordings, as well as ground truth labels detailing speech interruptions. The dataset is called SpeakFree. The results of the study indicate that precision in identifying speech interruptions using the proposed method reached 75%, surpassing alternative approaches that rely on time-delta features and accurate predictions. The proposed model, in conjunction with the SpeakFree dataset, presents a valuable component for developing speech-based reinforcement learning models, especially for training conversational systems, that incorporate the analysis of speech tempo as an essential component of the interaction. Most existing human action segmentation techniques rely heavily on annotated, supervised data to accurately detect temporal action occurrences in unseen data, but this approach is impractical and costly due to comprehensive annotation requirements. To overcome this challenge, we present SSCAP ($a.k.a.$ NoClick): a revolutionary, unsupervised action segmentation method that relies on sensorimotor activity maps to identify co-occurring actions in video footage. SSCAP generates and refines motion representations through sensorimotor self-supervision, ultimately allowing us to pinpoint action regions, determine their duration, and distinguish between classes. By leveraging a motion library and activity maps, our method also improves through co-occurring action sampling and parsing, thus reinforcing our representations. As a result of its effectiveness and efficiency, SSCAP outperforms state-of-the-art methods on challenging 10 datasets, surpassing prior works without accommodation for sensorimotor activity variability, noisy data, or inaccurate action segmentation. Notably, SSCAP successfully segments actions in videos with more than 3,000 frames and 200 actions without prior knowledge or pre-trained models. The conventional approach to assessing student performance in programming courses is quite elaborate. Despite its sophistication, studies have revealed that this method has significant flaws, such as focusing on task-oriented aspects and disregarding the overall learning process. As a result, instructors are unaware of the impact of their assessment strategies on student learning outcomes. Our study aims to address this knowledge gap by examining the effect of an assessment technique centered on conceptual understanding on student performance, as compared to a more traditional approach. Through an empirical analysis combining statistical process control and multiple linear regression, we investigated the connection between exam scores and various factors such as study time, perceived difficulty, and diversity in two university courses that employ a programming-based learning management system. The results show that student perception of exam difficulty is the only significant influence on exam performance, contradicting our initial hypothesis. Additionally, we found that conceptual focus in assessments does not adversely affect students' ability to grasp exam-specific concepts. This study sheds light on the shortcomings of a commonly used teaching method, highlighting its implications for instructors instead of improving students' learning process. The study's results can guide instructors on how to refine their assessment strategies, ultimately enhancing student performance. The study's findings are instrumental in generating hypotheses for future research on the topic. The non-classical properties of boson sampling setups persist over time due to quantum entanglement between photons, which explains their immeasurability using conventional methods, such as homodyne measurement. Our study delves into the phenomenon of entanglement in the state vector of boson sampling. To this end, we've developed a theoretical model based on a continuous-variable quantum random matrix theory approach, which accurately describes the entanglement present in the state vector, particularly its connection to the number of photons involved, the correlation order, and the total number of photons available. This theoretical model facilitates efficient numerical analysis, enabling assessments of NBS capabilities for various photon numbers, correlation degrees, and sample sizes, which can reach millions, an enormous difference from the current experimental limitations. Our results demonstrate a substantial entanglement presence, even in the reduced density matrix of photons, which becomes increasingly significant with larger correlation degrees. Moreover, the accuracy of quantum channels classification based on their reduced density matrices is shown to decline rapidly with increasing photon numbers. In addition, the study establishes a scaling limit for boson sampling set attainability in terms of the total photon number, correlation degree, and sample size, which can be utilized for experimental data recovery purposes, such as quantum tomography. Our results can potentially expand boson sampling set applications, contribute to the development of precise quantum channel classification tools, and enable the creation of future experimental protocols enhancing quantum channel classification accuracy. Furthermore, the study explores the entanglement of photons in the state vector of any Gaussian quantum system, enabling the theoretical modeling and subsequent numerical analysis of entanglement in Gaussian systems using photon statistical moments, which can be measured experimentally. Our results demonstrate a substantial entanglement presence even in the photon statistical moments, which becomes increasingly significant with larger correlation degrees. Moreover, the accuracy of quantum channels classification based on photon statistical moments and the corresponding classical models is shown to decline rapidly with increasing photon numbers. Our work may potentially expand the utilization of statistical moments in quantum research and classification. Finally, the study demonstrates that the presence of entanglement in the state vector of any Gaussian quantum system enables an accurate simulation of quantum classification processes using classical models based on random matrix theory approach. Our results demonstrate a substantial shift in the distortion of quantum classification error, from a linear to a logarithmic one, as the number of photons increases, which can be obtained efficiently due to the fast numerical convergence towards the mesoscopic regime. Supervised learning of temporal data is widely used but these methods are often hindered in their application to life sciences due to the necessity of labeling data, which can be costly and time-consuming, especially when dealing with large datasets. A major difficulty in using unsupervised methods for high-dimensional data is the lack of effective metrics to measure performance, particularly in systems where the target variable is not clearly defined. We propose using a mixture of guides with deep neural networks to overcome these issues by leveraging expert knowledge to improve high-dimensional temporal prediction performance. We test this approach with simulated data of varying levels of complexity and find that it outperforms other unsupervised methods across the board. Notably, the guide can be updated during training, allowing it to be used as a standalone method. Our results have significant implications for several fundamental problems in life sciences, such as inferring brief dynamics from time series data and reconstructing complete states from sparse data. Ultimately, this approach demonstrates superior performance over existing methods in these areas. It also exhibits significant improvements over supervised methods by requiring less data and avoiding dependencies on annotated data. Effective use of this approach requires guides with strong expert knowledge as well as systems with sufficient time series data and organizational complexity. We hypothesize that this approach will successfully apply to various other high-dimensional life science problems such as modeling protein structures and mitochondrial dynamics. Notably, the major limitations of this approach include its inability to handle data with missing values, limits imposed by the availability of guides, and dependencies on time series data complexity and organizational structure. Closed-source neural networks, found in devices such as smart speakers and smartphones, cannot be accessed due to security restrictions. Yet, learning models from these unaccessible networks is possible by sending update vectors through existing communication channels. Although useful for smart edge applications, this approach's efficiency relies on substantial communication, limiting its suitability to resource-constrained federated learning settings. To address these communication limitations and maintain security, we present a new decentralized recursive communication method. This approach offers multiple communication savings options, and we successfully apply several optimization techniques from the literature to reduce communication, while maintaining model accuracy. Experimental results using real-world image datasets confirm the effectiveness of our approach, resulting in up to a 10x reduction in communication, outperforming existing schemes. These findings motivate further research aimed at achieving both privacy and efficient communication for federated learning applications. The DP-REC code is available on GitHub at this link.
