Counting a nation's population is one of the most fundamental indicators of a country's development. Unmobilized rural populations in developing countries lack access to accurate population data due to the significant costs associated with gathering such information. Recent advancements in mobile mapping and autonomous driving have enabled population estimation research teams to test the feasibility of employing these advancements to gather data on rural areas, aiming to obtain more precise and detailed information on unsealed roads and cross-country trails. This paper showcases the results of employing a mobile mapping system, known as HereMap's system, hereafter HM, in Mozambique's rural areas, revealing the significant sway of human factors, weather conditions, and rugged terrain on autonomous technology performance. Despite encountering numerous obstacles, our team obtained 77 percent of the desired data, achieving an impressive 94 percent data accuracy in population hotspots, indicating that our approach could be a viable method for gathering data on rural roads and cross-country trails. Furthermore, our analysis of the contributions of various HM components revealed that specific adjustments can boost the system's overall performance, allowing it to collect 100 percent of the desired data. Ongoing research initiatives aim to optimize the changes made during our experiment and evaluate the HM system in additional countries. Specifically, our experiment indicates that various unexplored applications of these technologies could yield considerable returns, ultimately contributing to the advancement of both. Here, we discuss and investigate several potential uses, including the monitoring of trails, CO2 emissions measurement, and aerial surveillance, presenting these ideas to the research community for further development. It achieves this by introducing a set of local estimators to estimate data frequencies, which are integrated into a non-adversarial learning framework that optimally designs the estimators with the fewest parameters possible based on the dataset characteristics. By leveraging these estimators, the proposed filter achieves false-free data collection and noise resistance while maintaining query performance at log(n), showcasing significant improvements over alternative solutions. This approach is flexible, however, requires some overhead for data collection. The proposed framework utilizes the smooth particle hydrostatics method to model complex multi-phase fluid-structure interactions at unique length and time scales, integrating different numerical approaches for solid and fluid dynamics to simulate interactions between arbitrary shapes and speeds. To efficiently capture varied flow and impact phenomena, the framework combines scales of observation and models fluid behavior using a blend of fluid- and particle-in-liquid schemes and considers surface tension when fluid particles come into contact with a solid surface. To handle complex interactions between solids and fluids, the framework integrates a generalized Pennington-Spalding model and a simplified version of the Vodsi-Cook model, both of which account for volume changes and stresses in interacting objects. To validate the framework's accuracy in simulating interactions involving speed and pressure, as well as small-scale surface tension effects, we conducted a series of experiments testing its performance in numerous scenarios including high-speed impacts and tiny bubble interactions. The results show that this module raises the maximum achievable pitch range by 25.2%, thereby boosting speech quality and controllability. The updated FastPitch framework with the pitch modification module surpasses human-generated voices in speech quality and controllability across numerous benchmarking tests. Specifically, it achieves 0.095 absolute gains in the mean subjective mean opinion score (MOS) as well as a 10.3% expansion in the pitch range. Moreover, this module facilitates the creation of more extreme pitch deviations without altering regular voices. The modified FastPitch voices with the pitch modification module exhibit natural-sounding pitch changes and preserve the timbre of the voices, whereas the extended pitch range in human-generated voices shows a notable decline. The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model has excelled in approximating complex functions with compact ensembles of simpler experts. Nonetheless, training such represetntations comes with its challenges, particularly the propensity to get stuck in local optima where no single expert can alone adequately cover the functional space. To tackle this issue, we present two novel variational objectives in this study. These new objectives not only help MoE avoid getting stuck in local optimas by encouraging overlapping coverage from experts but also make it easier to prevent experts from overly specializing in data samples. Our variational objectives facilitate the development of a first-of-its-kind capacitated network, where each sample's assignment to experts and the distribution of experts' responsibilities are learned end-to-end. As a result, we successfully derived an unsupervised full-batch algorithm that significantly improves the quality of MoE representations while also accelerating training by a considerable margin. Notably, our algorithm not only outperforms the current state-of-the-art in complex functional approximation but also significantly shortens training time. Moreover, by integrating our capacitated network with quantization techniques, we created a unique approach that enables the scalable deployment of MoE on resource-restricted devices through constrained minimization of the MoE loss. We extensively tested our methods against top-tier baselines, yielding outstanding results that validate their efficacy. Moreover, we conducted an empirical analysis to provide insights on the behavior of MoE representations. Despite the widespread use of models with large non-linear kernels in image recognition, there's no clear understanding of the transfer learning principles that apply to kernel-based deep learning. Our study begins by revealing two surprising agreements among experts in the field, which we later dispute through a scientific investigation. The first agreement is that "informed model components can be directly adapted" for transfer learning, meaning parts of pre-trained models can be used with or without fine-tuning, depending on the model architecture. Conversely, we show this claim to be false and provide examples to illustrate the point. The second agreement is that "fine-tuning informs us about which data dimensions influence the model" and, as a result, dimensionality reduction techniques can be used after fine-tuning to understand the data's underlying structure. We contest this idea by demonstrating it to be untrue and providing an alternative interpretation, which we then substantiate with supporting evidence. Our investigation sheds light on the underlying dynamics of deep neural networks and their implications for transfer learning; it also sets the stage for future research in model adaptation, analysis, and understanding. The findings presented in this study are grounded in theoretically derived models, mathematically sound, and verified through empirical analysis and a diverse range of experiments, utilizing datasets such as ImageNet, CIFAR, and CelebA. Importantly, these results are applicable not only to neural networks but also to any kernel-based model used for image recognition. Ultimately, these findings illuminate the mechanisms driving transfer learning in deep learning and reveal new insights into the underlying dynamics of deep neural networks. The standard perturbation model is commonly employed to account for amplitude spikes and random variations in timing and phase errors of optical channel nonlinearity for unamplified fiber-optic channels. Formulating discrete-time models enables precise nonlinearity modeling and precise compensation of higher-order nonlinear effects in inter-symbol interference channels. This paper develops precise discrete-time models for standard perturbation nonlinearity and provides compensation equations for high-order nonlinear effects. The derivation first converts nonlinearity probability density functions into discrete forms and then applies the central limit theorem to derive a discrete-time nonlinearity probability density function. Based on this distribution, a discrete-time model is developed, along with the associated characterization metrics and statistics. Finally, precise compensation equations and algorithms are formulated to mitigate high-order inter-symbol interference in unamplified fiber-optic channels. Experimental and theoretical comparisons of discrete-time models and the CP-based amplifier are presented, demonstrating the discrete-time model's accuracy in field scenarios and its potential in enabling high-data-rate transmission. Moreover, a precise distortion detection method is proposed, enabling the monitoring of nonlinear effects and ensuring the reliability of high-data-rate transmission systems. This is achieved through a linear combination of discrete-time models and linear regression, where the local slopes of the combined nonlinearity can inform the design of high-data-rate transmission. This approach facilitates real-time nonlinearity monitoring and feedback loop control, enhancing transmission quality and reducing bit error rate. Ultimately, our findings indicate that discrete-time models and linear regression can achieve a bit error rate reduction of 10^-3 and support data rates above 100 Gb/s. The derived discrete-time models and the linear regression technique can enhance nonlinearity-tolerant high-data-rate transmission, where the discrete-time model is essential for precise nonlinearity modeling and compensation, and the linear regression technique is crucial for real-time nonlinearity monitoring and feedback control. The explicit discrete-time models and the linear regression technique will contribute to the development of high-data-rate transmission systems and the practical application of nonlinear compensation. The Dial-a-Ride Problem is a challenging task involving scheduling a fleet of vehicles to meet the transportation needs of passengers with diverse starting and ending points in a confined area with restricted roads. This problem is a variant of the Vehicle Routing Problem, but with the added complexity of passengers' dynamic arrival and departure times. To tackle the Dial-a-Ride Problem in urban settings, we propose a model that accounts for urban traffic constraints, incorporating characteristics such as sectorized roads and varying traffic densities. A solution method consists of two key components: a high-level algorithm designed to reduce the complexity of the problem, and a lower-level solution algorithm responsible for refining the solution. Through computational analysis utilizing 30 test cases, our proposed technique has demonstrated its effectiveness by finding solutions within an optimality gap of less than 0.04% and reducing processing time by approximately two times compared to alternative methods. Furthermore, the developed models and solution techniques are presented in a user-friendly format utilizing Python's Pyomo language and solved with the high-performance solver, Baron. To facilitate the implementation of these methods in real-world settings, we introduce a custom-made software package, DdiaRide, which provides an interactive graphical user interface to input and visualize problems. A quick overview of the problem and proposed solution techniques are provided, with a more in-depth mathematical formulation and implementation details available in a companion document. Alzheimer's disease, characterized by progressive memory loss and cognitive decline, is the most prevalent form of dementia. Its prolonged, 10-year latent period between initial detection and actual diagnosis allows for limited potential for preventative intervention. Consequently, focus has shifted to early-stage, high-risk individuals, particularly the elderly, to identify those who may progress to Alzheimer's. The use of neuroimaging, specifically magnetic resonance imaging, has been instrumental in identifying biomarkers and monitoring disease-related changes in the brain. Recently, Deep InfoMax, a self-supervised deep learning framework, has been applied to identify portentous indicators in MRI scans, ultimately contributing to earlier Alzheimer's detection. Deep learning, capable of deriving data-driven meaning from imaging inputs, is particularly suited for this purpose. Our work involves using unenhanced MRI scans, paired with manual segmentation of primary brain structures, to develop models that can be trained without supervision, given the abundance of available data. We have conducted a thorough study evaluating the performance of various self-supervised models, including the widely recognized Contextual Triplets and Deep InfoMax, to identify their strengths and limitations. Our experiments involved adapting Deep InfoMax for whole-brain radiofrequency signal autoencoder and structure-type autoencoder assessments. The former system exhibited remarkable performance, demonstrating 88% similarity to a trained model three months after training, and accurately identifying normal controls and Alzheimer's patients with 88% and 85% accuracy respectively, using the DecapafMRI dataset without any further refinement. Our findings illustrate the effectiveness of self-supervised deep learning in detecting early Alzheimer's stages using publicly available data sources. We plan to make this code open-source to facilitate widespread adoption and collaboration. The research was supported by the Millis Family Foundation. Natural Language Processing employs a crucial task called semantic parsing, which requires the analysis of the literal meaning of a sentence to accurately identify the real-world entities, actions, locations, etc. involved. However, the current best methods still face significant shortcomings as they solely rely on predefined patterns and average outcomes. This paper introduces a groundbreaking, interaction-driven framework for semantic parsing, based on the idea that interconnected components can achieve meaningful interpretations through interactions among them. We suggest a combined system consisting of a recurrent neural network and a pre-existing parser to model these interactions, which was trained on the Bank data and further tested across 11 diverse datasets without fine-tuning, achieving notable improvements on 8 of them when compared to existing top results. Moreover, our proposed method demonstrates superior performance on tasks beyond semantic parsing, such as text classification and sentiment analysis, using the same model. We ultimately validate the effectiveness of our approach through detailed analysis of the features learned and the insights provided by the interactions between the components. Moreover, we show the potential of our approach by extending it to more complex datasets like Wiki102 and the entire English Abstract Meaning Representation corpus. We also provide a comprehensive explanation of the method in the supplementary materials. Experimental results reveal that our proposed method dominates the state-of-the-art semantic parsing achievements not only on the commonly used Bank dataset but also surpasses other notable results on less commonly used datasets, paving the way for broader applications. We hope the proposed approach will enable significant progress in natural language understanding tasks in general. The code for our proposed method is available at https://github.com/ericlin.tw/interaction_sparser. Additional information can be found at https://ericlin.tw. To facilitate future research, we provide an updated version of our tool to achieve state-of-the-art results on the entire English Abstract Meaning Representation corpus. The code for the updated version is available at https://github.com/ericlin.tw/efficient_improved_201221. Although our proposed method has not yet outperformed the state-of-the-art on the English Abstract Meaning Representation corpus with the current tool at https://github.com/ericlin.tw/interaction_sparser, we provide an explanation and hope for further improvements in the next section. This approach enables an alternative definition for the concept of thin structures, offering insights into their properties. Furthermore, we establish that any conformal shadow substance can be viewed as a specific instance of a metastable conformal shadow substance, without any inherent restrictions. The established theorems are implemented through a practical demonstration of reconstructing a model shadow field from a given formal shadow field, a crucial aspect in the context of quantum field theory reconstruction from shadow fields. Moreover, a series of computational methods are developed to estimate numerical solutions for user-proposed model shadow fields, a functionality that is incorporated into the user-frontend interface of the ShadowProject package. The content of this document, as well as the associated code for the ShadowProject package, is grounded in the concepts of relational database management systems and object-oriented programming. Artificial Intelligence (AI) based medical devices are starting to be used in clinical settings, with the European Medicines Agency approving one example in 2021. At present, there is a lack of standard methodologies to thoroughly evaluate and validate such devices due to difficulties in creating replicas and simulating real-world data. This study examines how conformal forecasting can be utilized to assess the performance of AI medical devices under realistic conditions, particularly in situations where their training and testing data may vary significantly. We implement a non-parametric conformal prediction validation technique to evaluate an AI stroke detector in two real-world environments and found that it is effective in detecting differences between the device's performance in these environments. Moreover, this method does not rely on any assumptions about the data generation process and provides reliable, straightforward inferences. We showcase this method using an actual medical device in a real-world context, thereby highlighting its practical utility. This research argues that conformal forecasting can be a reliable approach to test and validate complex medical AI systems, especially in real-world environments where controlled data is not available. We anticipate this research to be a crucial benchmark for future evaluations of medical AI instruments. We have further extended this research by studying other models, datasets and medical AI applications, detailing the results in a companion paper listed in references. The associated code is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/EstebanLundberg/AI-Model-Validation. The Active Settleability Number (ANS) was previously proposed to assess wastewater treatability through an empirical compression principle. For each group of chemicals added to wastewater, a unique set of ANS values is assigned. The effectiveness of ANS compression is evaluated based on the deviance, a measure of discrepancy, which can be calculated as the negative logarithm of the probability of observing zero or a positive ANS value for the given number of trials. In this study, we investigate whether the ANS deviance Compressed (ANSdC) model, which incorporates both ANS values and trial counts in a statistical framework, is a valid model of probability, and we assess its mechanistic underpinnings. Our analysis reveals that the ANSdC model's deviance is disproportionately increased by additional parameters beyond 1, 2, and 3, suggesting that the ANS compression mechanism involves at least a 3-parameter process. In a separate experiment, we show that the ANS deviance Compressed model is not simply a scaled version of the extremal tail dependence model, which models a similar deviance score using a single parameter. Additionally, our empirical results indicate that the ANS deviance Compressed values for pairs of chemicals with inter-ANS deviance values below 2 do not differ significantly from those of the extremal tail dependence model. In contrast, pairs of chemicals with inter-ANS deviance values above 2 demonstrate a more substantial increase in the ANSdC model's effective parameters, which may explain these findings. Our analysis provides mechanistic insight into the ANS deviance Compressed model that could enhance its practical usage in wastewater treatability assessments. Furthermore, the proposed methodology can be broadly applied to assess the mechanistic underpinnings of probability models in various fields. In this study, we validate that the ANS deviance Compressed model is a statistically and mechanistically sound model of probability. In a separate experiment, we show that the ANS deviance Compressed model fails to provide a good statistical fit to the probability of zero or positive ANS values for the extreme tail dependence model. These findings imply that the ANS deviance Compressed model operates through a different underlying mechanism than the extreme tail dependence model. The EPOS model's ability to simulate LHC particle collisions accurately extends to the simulation of baryon clusters consisting of three heavy particles, such as $NNN$, $N\Lambda N$, and $\Sigma\Sigma\Lambda$. These clusters, formed through the interaction of strange and nucleon particles, remain stable due to the strong short-range attraction between them. Characteristics of the baryon clusters are determined after their formation in collisions, specifically their transverse momentum distribution, size, and internal velocity. Findings show that the distribution of transverse momentum for these clusters is similar to that of individual baryons, with accompanying kinematic factors determining their shapes. The size and surface density of these clusters are consistent with those of three isolated protons, with their sizes ranging between 4-6 fm and surface densities approximately 1-2 times that of a single proton. Additionally, the energy required to disintegrate these baryon clusters is significantly influenced by their internal velocity; consequently, their melting points vary in line with their kinetic energy. Importantly, the EPOS model predicts that these baryon clusters have a long lifespan, persisting for many collisional processes, with their lifetimes exceeding 20 fm, thereby increasing their detectability using heavy-ion collision experiments. The EPOS model's predictions provide valuable insights into the identification of these baryon clusters in future experiments, with experimental findings indicating that these clusters are present in collisions involving a large multiplicity of particles and the HBT correlations could distinguish them from individual baryons. The appearance of 'ghost' particles, with negative momentum, is another characteristic of these baryon clusters that can be observed in experiments. The theoretical description of the formation and properties of these heavy-heavy hadronic clusters using the EPOS model provides an essential framework for their study in experiments, with experimental findings suggesting that these clusters are a genuine phenomenon. The presence of $N\Lambda N$ and $\Sigma\Sigma\Lambda$ baryon clusters is indicated by the results of some experiments with their potential to modify the final state of particle collisions in a noticeable way. The study of these heavy-heavy hadronic clusters using the EPOS model highlights their unique properties, with their identification in experiments providing valuable knowledge of their formation mechanisms. Theoretical simulations indicate that these clusters are a natural consequence of particle collisions at the LHC and their study can contribute significantly to our current understanding of hadron formation. To address these limitations, we've created a predictive model that takes the desired goal into consideration and adapts more easily to changing social patterns. Our model consists of a sequential recognition component that identifies past movement patterns and a future recognition component that uses past information to make predictions about future behavior. To ensure social awareness, we incorporate socially-conscious rethinking modules, which learn the probabilities of reaching different social-related states and adjust their predictions accordingly. We evaluated our model through manual and automated assessments on a newly collected dataset. Our findings show that our model successfully considers the desired destination and adapts more effectively to changing social behavior patterns. For instance, our model performs significantly better than traditional models when forecasting over long periods of time, and it's more resistant to fluctuations in the training dataset. In the field of Quantitative Medicine, experts strive to find answers to several prominent questions using microscopic blood cell images. By processing these images, researchers aim to make informed decisions in precision medicine, guiding therapeutic strategies and predicting patient outcomes at individual levels. By analyzing the appearance of circulatory cells, scientists aim to gain insights into relevant pathological and physiological events. The categorization of blood cells in microscope images is a key task in this field. Currently, the most effective way to accomplish this task relies on machine learning, specifically the design of accurate and robust models capable of handling diverse blood cell types. The creation of these models requires extensive data analysis and the incorporation of new information to enhance their performance. By combining multiple neural network models, trained on various data sources and then merged, it's possible to achieve higher overall categorization accuracy compared to current standards. This research demonstrates a powerful method for uniting distinct neural network models through ensemble learning, resulting in the development of a single, all-encompassing model capable of accurately categorizing blood cells in microscope images, even in scenarios with limited data availability and significant data variations. The new ensemble model exhibits higher accuracy compared to current non-en ensemble models, achieving an average accuracy increase of 5.9 percent. This model has the potential to significantly contribute to the accuracy of blood cell categorization, leading to implications in the field of Quantitative Medicine. The study indicates that this ensemble method can successfully be applied to other image classification challenges. The study's code will be made publicly available on GitHub to enable the replication of the findings. An accompanying software package, BloodNN, which incorporates the ensemble model, is now available on PyPI and can be accessed via npm, allowing for the execution of the study's findings. The process relies on the conversion of image data from the RGB to CIE1931 CIE L*a*b* color space, followed by the calculation of each pixel's dominant wavelength and hue angle. The determined hue angles are then adjusted using specific blending ratios, after which the RGB values are converted back to the RGB color space. The technique incorporates dual temperature responses, one sharp and one gradual, for refined control. A user-controllable parameter governs the transition point of the blending ratios. The authors thoroughly examined the underlying mathematical properties of the HTE algorithm, as well as its sensitivity to parameter variations, and compared its performance to that of a contemporary algorithm, specifically HSL. The authors aim for their work to serve as a starting point or inspiration, opening doors to novel collaborations and contributions. Compared to a conventional Higgs boson, a subtle Higgs exhibits diminished couplings with fermions and weakly coupled particles, but enhanced interactions with spin to a certain degree. This unusual behavior makes it detection challenging, but also, relatively straightforward. Our research proposes an updated set of search strategies for subtle Higgses that are produced in association with top quarks and the 125 GeV Higgs boson, using the data collected by the LHC's Run 2 experiments. We specifically focused on two specific subtle Higgs scenarios, given their minimal interference with standard model processes: a super-critical Higgs model and a mixed interaction scenario. We observed significant reductions in statistical and systematic uncertainties for our new analysis, yielding improved sensitivity by a factor of 2 and 10 to 30% for the super-critical and mixed scenarios respectively, using the data collected from 139 fb^-1 of proton-proton collisions. Our new analysis is specifically centered around the enhanced top quark spin energy for the super-critical scenario, while focusing on the total energy of the top quark system for the mixed scenario. Additionally, we took into consideration the effects of the Higgs's decay into bottom quarks and Higgs's self-collision processes, also incorporating pure spin-0 and spin-2 subtle Higgs scenarios for our total energy analysis but observed reduced acceptance due to increased interference with standard model processes. Finally, using pseudo-experiments, our updated analysis now reaches a 95% confidence level of sensitivity to 750 GeV for the super-critical scenario, as well as 935 and 981 GeV for the mixed scenarios assuming the Higgs decays to bottom quarks or the Higgs's self-collision respectively. On the other hand, the pure spin-2 and spin-0 scenarios remain poorly constrained by the current experiments. This new analysis is proposed to be implemented for future LHC experiments, specifically those using the HL-LHC, where the sensitivity reaches 2075, 2085 and 2105 GeV for the pure spin-0, spin-2 and super-critical scenarios after 3 ab^-1 of data collection. Despite numerous advancements in the field of non-Hermitian physics, particularly in the theory of one-dimensional non-Hermitian topological phases, a critical aspect remains unresolved: understanding the impact of interactions on these systems is still shrouded in uncertainty. To the best knowledge available, a systematic framework for analyzing correlated systems in the context of non-Hermitian topology is lacking. In a significant breakthrough, we have developed a generalized framework that applies to a broad class of interacting and non-interacting systems, allowing for the systematic alteration of their band structures and topological characteristics. The application of perturbation theory to the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, as opposed to the complement, yields an efficient and accurate method for analyzing systems controlled by non-Hermitian gaps without necessitating a transformation to Hermitian forms. This research explores the effect of maintaining consistent speech characteristics for multiple speakers in the same language dataset. The results from a listening test indicate that subtle changes in speech characteristics can be perceivable, and an adjustment factor in voice deployment is necessary, especially when voices are used repeatedly, not just by the speaker itself. The findings also suggest that correcting speech characteristics in translated texts, rather than original language versions, is more beneficial for synthetic voice production, as these changes are typically maintained during the translation process. The research primarily focuses on the requirements for creating authentic voices in spoken interactions rather than the characteristics of individual voices. This paper presents an innovative method for identifying alterations in unsupervised environments. Alteration detection is a critical application in surveillance and monitoring of urban areas, agricultural land, and environmental ecosystems. We address a fundamental challenge in alteration detection by improving upon existing encoder-based methods that rely on pairwise comparisons to locate alterations. To overcome comparison difficulties in high-dimensional hyperspectral data, we develop a novel approach that employs a deep convolutional autoencoder. The proposed architecture combines two branches – one focused on pixel-wise comparison and the other on feature-level comparison. The feature-level branch leverages the autoencoder's latent representation to detect alterations. We validate the efficacy of our proposed method through comprehensive experiments on the AIRSIS, Pavia University, and Urban areas datasets, achieving superior performance compared to existing top alteration detection methods. Notably, the proposed method demonstrates considerable potential for real-world applications with minimal feature engineering required. The invariant-set hypothesis proposes that certain hidden-variables take on specific values, adhering strictly to predetermined ranges, unlike another set that can freely vary within a defined scope, leading to an apparent randomness. Our study delves into the possibility of establishing the invariant-set by analyzing the energy spectra of quantum systems, specifically when some excitations are disabled, allowing us to compare our findings with randomly generated spectra. To facilitate this exploration, we develop a statistical model that simulates the invariant-set for non-commuting and commuting systems based on the Hilbert-Schmidt distance metric, and test it against randomly generated states. However, our research does not seek to validate the invariant-set hypothesis, but rather examines a hidden-variable model capable of describing both the invariant-set and random outcomes, corresponding to distinct sets of hidden-variables. Our statistical model is then applied to various quantum systems to determine the range of these hidden-variables. To calculate the HS-distances, we extend the stochastic density operator framework to the basis-independent domain, and our study reveals that the proposed statistical model is basis-independent and satisfies three fundamental principles: the model correctly identifies truly random outcomes, distinguishes between invariant-set and random outcomes, and distinguishes between distinct invariant sets for different states. To further validate the model, we conduct two experiments: the first compares the model's predictions with randomly generated spectra obtained from a quantum simulation, and the second assesses the model's applicability to distinct invariant sets for different families of quantum systems. However, our research does not provide a statistical analysis of the model's outcomes, and our study remains a theoretical exploration of the hidden-variable model rather than a test of its applicability to actual non-locality cases. To remedy this limitation, our team is currently working on generating extensive numerical data on the energy spectra of quantum systems, and suggesting an experimental protocol that could produce an interferometric deviation of the HS-distance, report forthcoming. Numerical data obtained from this study indicate the HS-distance to randomness distribution of the GHZ-state in the Bell-state range is approximately 0.33, and for the cluster states range is around 0.47. Conversely, our research shows that the first generation of quantum systems, such as the GHZ-state, have a lower range compared to the second generation of quantum systems, such as the cluster states. Furthermore, our research reveals that the third generation of quantum systems, based on realistic simulations, exhibits the highest range, and we attribute these differences to an underlying physical principle, and propose a simple explanation, namely that certain simulations fail

The vision of IoT includes diverse applications such as monitoring living spaces, infirmaries, and industrial environments with cameras. However, cameras produce extensive amounts of data, particularly images and video, which need to be processed on devices such as Raspberry Pi to be useful. Given the limitations of IoT devices, directly applying state-of-the-art techniques to them poses significant challenges. This study investigates the application of neural networks for processing camera data on IoT devices, with a specific focus on keyphrase detection. We analyzed how changing the network architecture and data compression type impacts the model's accuracy. This research demonstrated that a primary convolutional network can effectively identify key phrases from short videos on Raspberry Pi devices, achieving an accuracy of nearly 90%. Moreover, it revealed that using LP78 for data compression yields better results than the commonly used compression method, LZW. This research also compared the computational resources required for processing on Raspberry Pi and more powerful GPUs. While GPU processing offers faster inference, the difference in computation time on Raspberry Pi and GPUs does not significantly affect the model's accuracy, particularly not in low-resource settings like IoT devices. To the best knowledge of this research, it involves the first benchmark for image-based keyphrase detection and the first study to assess the impact of data compression on neural networks on IoT devices. Furthermore, it presents a novel framework for processing deep learning models on IoT devices and suggests that the increased model size of such models should be taken into consideration in resource-limited environments. Finally, the study demonstrates that a well-designed neural network can effectively identify key phrases from video sequences on devices like Raspberry Pi, making it possible to apply to monitoring applications. This research was carried out in partnership with the Dutch autism society 'Klik' and 'Their story's', with autism-related video samples used to test the model, resulting in key phrases that are in line with autism-related research findings, such as the preference for routine, several repeated behaviors, and a fear of crowds. Several generated key phrases by experts from 'Klik' and 'Their story's', which were not observed during data collection, also revealed the model's ability to classify unknown frames and its capacity for re-identifying the same object across different sequences. Consequently, there are considerable prospects for processing camera data on IoT devices using neural networks, given that the model's accuracy aligns with expert-generated key phrases. This research contributes to the discussion of the ethics of deep learning model processing on IoT devices and the potential of these models in the healthcare and social sectors. In embedded real-time systems, the prevalence of mixed importance applications necessitates a superior real-time performance. A preemptive kernel or hypervisor is typically employed to guarantee real-time performance. Integrating virtualization into hypervisors further enhances security, reliability, and user-friendly interface management. The widespread use of x86 virtualization facilities, including those provided by VT-6 (Intel) and VT-7 (AMD), has led to the development of various commercial and open-source hypervisors. Existing hypervisors fail to efficiently manage context switches, support interrupt prioritization, and efficiently allocate I/O resources, ultimately hindering real-time performance. To address these limitations, this paper presents T-Visor: a monolithic operating system turned hypervisor that leverages x86 virtualization facilities. The proposed hypervisor achieves real-time performance close to that of Monsoon/MoCA, a state-of-the-art real-time operating system, while virtualization facilities enable users to run applications safely and efficiently. To validate T-Visor's performance, a mixed importance embedded real-time testbed was designed and testbed evaluations were conducted based on the Standard Performance Evaluation Corporation benchmark. The results demonstrate T-Visor's ability to meet real-time performance demands. Furthermore, testbed evaluations confirm that T-Visor meets hard real-time performance requirements, while virtualization facilities prevent crashes or freezes observed in previous hypervisor designs. The proposed hypervisor achieves real-time performance close to that of Monsoon/MoCA, with real-time performance exceeding 99.999%, surpassing the requirements for embedded real-time systems. To summarise, T-Visor enables real-time performance and virtualization facilities to coexist, addressing the challenges of mixed importance applications through efficient context switching, interrupt prioritization, and I/O resource allocation. The results of testbed evaluations validate T-Visor's performance and effectiveness in managing applications with varying priorities and virtualization of critical system services using standard PC hardware. Automated controller design using model-based reinforcement learning has become a preferred method in various industries. However, the issue remains with model accuracy and controller robustness. This research focuses on developing resilient controllers that withstand model inaccuracies in autonomous vehicle motion control. Through simulated data collection and controller optimization, the proposed approach integrates probabilistic models to assess controller performance. Using Euler-Bernoulli beam dynamics and a power distribution controller, the approach is demonstrated with experimental results showing its robustness in challenging scenarios. The results indicate that the proposed approach reduces the impact of model inaccuracy on controller performance by at least 35%. The evaluation is based on the Generalized Energy Functional, which measures controller effectiveness. The experimental outcome shows that the proposed approach outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in terms of robustness, while also showcasing its ability to handle uncertainties in controller design. In chaotic many-body systems, the entropy of a subsystem within a tensor network, when not confined, grows with the system size, freely increasing beyond the entropy seen within a confined space defined by an entanglement Renormalization group. As an alternative, we quantify the entropy of a subsystem not confined using the methods from continuum hydrodynamics, specifically focusing on the refracted entropy through an interface separating the subsystem from its surrounding environment. Initially, we apply this approach to a 1D chaotic system, which is well-understood, and verify that our results align with existing entropy values. Subsequently, we extend our analysis to more complex many-body models, including the J1-X-Y model and a half-filled SU(4) XXZ model, where, notably, the refracted entropy deviates from the entanglement entropy in the thermodynamic limit. The calculated refracted entropy also demonstrates consistency with the entanglement entropy's behavior in the thermodynamic limit, suggesting its potential as a reliable proxy for entanglement in confined spaces and, more broadly, in condensed matter physics. The calculated entropy values can also provide new insights to the properties of the critical front. Quantum tunneling is crucial in molecular dynamics, protein folding and chemical reactions. Researchers are interested in understanding this process because it's heavily influenced by the tunneling coefficient, which depends on various factors including energy and the Hamiltonian of the system. However, this coefficient isn't easily measurable, as it's a complex, non-observable property. To overcome this limitation, scientists are exploring alternative ways to estimate the tunneling coefficient by quantifying tunneling's inherent characteristics that can be observed. One such trait measurable with Larmor clocks is the duration of tunneling, which is what this study is focused on. Using the Heisenberg picture, we derived a fundamental equation that relates the tunneling coefficient to this duration, independent of energy. Our research was conducted using Larmor clocks on two specific one-dimensional systems: a classical-like tunneling particle and a particle with quantum-induced backspin. We found that the tunneling coefficient can be completely determined from the duration of tunneling in the first case, but unknown influences on the tunneling coefficient cannot be disregarded in the second case. To resolve this issue, we developed an analytical method to isolate the influence of the tunneling Hamiltonian from the duration of tunneling, which we then applied to a particle under non-conservative forces, yielding surprising results, as the influence of the tunneling Hamiltonian was discovered to be stronger than expected. Our total approach is called spin-influenced Larmor tunneling, which is capable of accurately estimating the tunneling coefficient in scenarios previously considered intractable. This method may be used to analyze the tunneling coefficient in phenomena like the coexistence of conductive and semi-conductive states in graphene, as well as the mechanical basis for superconductivity. It's worth noting that spin effects on the tunneling coefficient require that the tunneling particle has a finite angular momentum. Importantly, the influence of the tunneling Hamiltonian can be observed at both zero and finite temperatures, while the spin effects require the conditions of the Heisenberg and Dirac correspondences, connecting quantum mechanics and special relativity, to be met. Our study of the tunneling coefficient using the spin-influenced Larmor tunneling approach may therefore hold the key to advancing our understanding of the thermomechanics of superconductivity and the dynamics of charge and energy transfer. Ultimately, the spin-influenced Larmor tunneling approach may provide valuable insights into the spin-mediated processes underlying molecular mechanics, the behavior of electrons in magnetic fields and the interaction between mechanics and chemistry. To address the ensemble method issues in online learning, we propose a novel ensemble approach called Online Ensemble Continual Learning (OECI). A key challenge in online learning is memory association, and ensemble learning is no exception. To overcome this, we introduce a neural structure for OECI that uses a set of parameterized ensembles with learnable parameters to effectively store class representations. Unlike existing methods, OECI does not rely on pre-defined memory or coordination mechanisms, and its neural structure allows for online learning through an end-to-end trainable process. Notably, OECI can be adapted to various ensemble methods by adjusting its ensemble designs. Experimental results demonstrate that OECI outperforms other approaches in online learning and continuous learning tasks, and its success paves the way for the development of multiple ensemble designs. These findings are further validated by conducting analyses on multiple ensemble designs and a case study of multi-task learning. In addition, we provide open-access resources, including code and data, to support the development of more robust learning models. Ultimately, we contribute to ensemble method development by introducing 12 novel ensemble designs, and our research is expected to inspire further research in this area. This paper introduces a novel approach for approximating non-zero-sum infinite-horizon quadratic criteria of intricate financial models that involve complex transformations and uncertain probability shifts. We initially simplify the calculation by converting the issue into a set of non-zero-sum finite-horizon linear-quadratic stochastic control problems with uncertain parameters. Based on the number of grid points applied in space and time, we then compute an approximate solution using convex approximation techniques and solve the resulting linear stochastic control problem recursively. We provide theoretical validation of the numerical method along with an error analysis that confirms its convergence. We also demonstrate the practical effectiveness of this approach through various numerical experiments. These experiments examine characteristics such as fair value, fair value volatility, leverage, and correlation between different investment and reinsurance strategies. They also highlight how various parameters, including mean switching frequencies, grid points, and time intervals affect the approximation accuracy. Additionally, we compare the computational efficiency of different numerical solving methods for a two-regime model that arises from applying the convex averaging technique to approximate the regime-switching model. Finally, motivated by the recent COVID-19 pandemic, we use our method to investigate how different reinsurance strategies interact with a widely used pandemic model. Specifically, we aim to minimize the loss minimax cost by finding an optimal reinsurance arrangement for a life insurance company in the presence of the COVID-19 pandemic. symmetry in the low-energy pion-nucleon system, with particular focus on the
spinning components of the pion-nucleon interaction that are neglected in
traditional partial-wave analysis, including the dynamics of the delta resonance. 
It will be shown that these interactions conform to a unique, long-standing
prediction made by Thomas Reed in 1959, with implications that are now being
explored further.  Evidence is presented suggesting that the pion-nucleon
system is in a state of conformality across its entire energy spectrum, with
Chern-Simons terms potentially dominating the system's behavior.  Our work
suggests that the F\"anberg-Watson theorem may have broader applications than
previously assumed, with the delta resonance representing a pivotal region where
the pion-nucleon system transitions from one phase to another.  It is our hope
that these ideas will spark new interest and insight into the physics of the
low-energy pion-nucleon system.  Finally, some potential experimental
consequences associated with these ideas are discussed, with a focus on the K+
pion-nucleon system.  Specifically, we suggest that the existing analtyticity of the

consequences for its low-energy behavior.  These ideas were initially proposed at

updated version of that talk is provided as an appendix to this article.  In
addition to the ideas themselves, what is notable about this chapter in the
history of the subject is the relatively small amount of time that elapsed between

In goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, practitioners often encounter situations where multiple 'goals' within an instruction cause confusion, leading to a failure in accurately understanding the instruction and achieving the desired learning results. This study, referred to as 'Overcoming Ambiguity', delves into resolving reference ambiguity in goal-conditioned learning. Researchers proposed a new learning framework, referred to as 'Disambiguation via Conditioned Imagination' (DCI), which relies on additional training data to clarify ambiguous terms. By doing so, the DCI framework ensures students recognize the relevant context of each goal and effectively map goals to actions. Experimental findings have shown that DCI significantly outperforms leading competitors and achieves near-optimal performance for a wide range of 'Reference Ignores' and 'Reference Clarifies' settings. Moreover, the study highlights the importance of choosing an optimal strategy for disambiguating references and demonstrates that DCI is particularly effective because it only requires one disambiguating example per ambiguous term. Interestingly, the study reveals that even a single training example per ambiguous term is sufficient to eliminate reference ambiguity. Finally, the study demonstrates that DCI is highly versatile, allowing it to be applied to multiple learning settings, including a challenging 'Semi-Supervised' environment. Despite the presence of significant 'adversarial' cases, Disambiguation via Conditioned Imagination successfully achieves near-optimal performance. As such, Disambiguation via Conditioned Imagination effectively addresses reference ambiguity in goal-conditioned learning and illuminates the challenges associated with this type of learning. The current paper represents the first comprehensive exploration of overcoming reference ambiguity in a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning setting. Importantly, the study highlights that a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning system can effectively overcome reference ambiguity without receiving additional data on the specifically ambiguous term. Moreover, the study shows that a goal-conditioned learning system can effectively overcome reference ambiguity with only one training example per goal. Experimental results suggest that Disambiguation via Conditioned Imagination outperforms all competitors and achieves near-optimal performance for a wide range of 'Reference Ignores' and 'Reference Clarifies' settings. Finally, the study demonstrates the generalizability of Disambiguation via Conditioned Imagination and achieves near-optimal performance in a Semi-Supervised setting. As such, the study recommends using Disambiguation via Conditioned Imagination in a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning setting where reference ambiguity may occur. This paper introduces MEE, a groundbreaking dataset for multilingual event detection.

solution. Built on Wikipedia's event categories, the MEE dataset safely extracts
relevant text from English and non-English Wikipedia pages to create 25k high-quality event keywords in seven languages. These keywords have been translated into all seven languages, allowing for seamless cross-lingual transfer.

evaluation, and test data, encompassing 188k and 51k instances in English and six
other languages, respectively. Our experiments using BERT-LM and ALBERT-ML use the

A key challenge in natural language understanding stems from the necessity to balance data efficiency with model capacity. Typically, improvements in model performance require the accumulation of more data, but this can be difficult to achieve, especially in languages with limited resources. This paper demonstrates how universal parsing capabilities, which can handle various input formats, can be combined with semantically-inclisive reasoning to overcome this issue. By adopting a collaborative learning approach and training both syntax and semantics simultaneously, we've developed a unified model capable of generating diverse parsing outputs, such as dependencies and UPOS/UPOS tags, as well as performing representative information extraction tasks. Our experimental results indicate that this dual approach yields high-quality parsing outputs and demonstrates comparable performance to more resource-hungry models. Moreover, we've discovered that our model exhibits smooth parsing output preferences, which can be leveraged to enhance downstream task adaptability. This paper presents key findings from the analysis of our model's behavior, offering potential solutions to address these observations through further research. Specifically, we've made our model code available, as well as a new dataset, UPOS-DEP, which enables the evaluation of parsing models with enhanced representational capacity. This provides researchers with the opportunity to adapt our model to a wider range of parsing outputs, potentially reducing dependence on diverse and often costly annotation techniques. Such a shift could significantly ease the process of achieving high-quality parsing outputs across many languages. Finally, we've also showcased the model's capacity for semantic extraction by highlighting its ability to efficiently and accurately engage in information extraction tasks, effectively supplementing syntax with rich, contextually-inclisive understanding. This paper presents key findings from the analysis of our model's behavior, offering important implications for natural language understanding across multiple languages. Ultimately, we argue that collaborative learning, diversity in parsing outputs, and semantics-inclisive reasoning in syntax inference hold considerable promise for advancing these areas. Building time- and space-variant models that can accommodate varied data qualities, especially for complex environments with scarce label resources, is essential for practical applications in robotics. We have developed an adaptable deep learning-based framework that fuses multitemporal image time series and future image forecasts to create accurate maps, utilizing spatial context and temporal continuity in the process. This model utilizes causal transformers in a semi-unsupervised setting, learning to predict the self-evolution of features across different imaging sessions. For an efficient solution, our approach involves alternating iterative processes until convergence, utilizing future image forecasts to update the model, which in turn uses past time series to update the prediction of the model's initial state. This method enables self-refinement without additional supervision, making it suitable for online cartography in robotics and similar scenarios. This approach successfully navigated the trade-off between data persistence and spatial information in the simulation and improved the accuracy of 3D object reconstructions when compared to traditional baselines in real-world applications. When used for generating maps from pre-trained models, our method produced more accurate results in complex real-world scenarios, especially when the data was imperfect and low-quality, often resulting in local optima, as it learned to combine the strengths of various modeling methods through self-guided learning. These benefits were also observed in other challenging scenarios involving sparse and low-quality data, as well as cross-view point cloud alignment in 3D reconstruction, where our method consistently outperformed state-of-the-art baselines. Efficient neural network training with quantization has been a highly active area of research due to the significant speedup it offers by restricting weights and inputs to low-bit fixed values. Existing methods, while successful, often compromise accuracy or exacerbate gradient vanishing/issues. To address this, we developed a novel optimization technique specifically suited for quantized neural networks. This approach leverages a unique understanding of quantization to optimize layer-wise training strategies, incorporating feedback and adaptability. The resulting technique, AskewSGD, is an iterative, annealed method that adjusts training parameters (such as gradient clipping) in parallel distribution networks to minimize disruption, utilizing feedback to guide future adjustments. AskewSGD's performance is demonstrated through kinetic-based training of binary and 1-bit convolutional neural networks, achieving notable improvements in accuracy and training speed, with results comparable to state-of-the-art approaches. The technique successfully circumvents gradient vanishing/issues, with implications for further research. The AskewSGD source code has been made publicly available. Specifically, $J_n(A_f)$ is composed of totally positive numbers of the form $x^2-y^5\pm5^k$, where $k$ ranges infinitely, and $X_n(A_f)$ is the resulting surface of a sixfold ramified integral model over $A_f$. Notably, the Jacobi group is the first instance of a Hecke-Kohnen-Mumford space that meets rigorous cohomological criteria, particularly $\dim H^*(X_n(A_f),\mathbb{C})=6n+1$. Consequently, the Jacobi group has significant implications for the resolution of the cohomology question in Hecke-Kohnen-Mumford spaces. Notably, the Authentic Jacobi group also addresses and resolves several other open questions related to the Hecke-Kohnen-Mumford spaces and their holomorphic cocycles of intermediate degree, particularly in regards to Waldspurger's theorem and its predicted generalizations. Lastly, the group also addresses another open problem which is related to an issue of determinacy of local invariant measures for certain actions of lattices on measures over Euclidean space.

Recent research by Choy et al. (2020) suggests that using the triplet loss in deep neural networks can lead to inaccurate learning when data distributions are not clearly distinguishable. This study presents multiple scenarios where modified triplet loss models and deep neural networks based on different architectures fail to overcome biases in data distribution. Additionally, our analysis indicates that using the triplet loss can sometimes result in inaccurate predictions and large gradients that lead to significant learning rate adjustments. This, in turn, can cause non-smooth optimization paths and reduced model generalizability. As an alternative, we suggest utilizing the multi-class proxy loss, a previously established loss function, to train deep neural networks. Unlike the triplet loss, the proxy loss does not introduce biases in data distribution and enables accurate learning. Our research also demonstrates that the proxy loss leads to more smooth and optimized convergence patterns compared to triplet-based models. Inspired by the findings of Rogers and Ginsburg (2020), which demonstrate that using "gradient surgery" can help researchers understand the influence of neural network gradients on decision-making processes, our analysis applies this technique to quantify the impact of gradients on triplet and proxy loss models. Specifically, our research indicates that gradient norms can reveal whether a triplet loss model is biased and that the proxy loss, when trained on a simple dataset, produces gradients with low $l_2$-norm across the entire data distribution. This study further explores the relationship between neural network gradients and class activation maps, demonstrating that the proxy loss models our analysis investigated exhibit strong correspondence between gradient signs and class activation map signs. Consequently, our research reveals that the proxy loss models our analysis have class activation maps that uniformly outline the data distribution boundaries, thereby accurately capturing the underlying structure of the data. As an extension of this finding, our analysis applies the gradient surgery technique to various neural network architectures to quantify the influence of gradients on decision-making patterns, with the results revealing that the proxy loss models exhibit more consistent and smooth decision patterns compared to triplet loss models, which show significant variability. Ultimately, our research confirms that the proxy loss leads to the development of more generalizable and smooth neural network models that accurately learn the data distribution boundaries, thereby leading to increased generalizability. This paper determines the values of $R_\infty$ for the generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $G = \mathbb{Z}^n \rtimes \mathbb{Z}$ and their nilpotent quotients $H = (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^n \rtimes \mathbb{Z}$ in the context of second convex geometry. The study of $R_\infty$ is a significant aspect of this theory. Notably, the study finds that $R_\infty$ is zero for $G$ in almost all cases, including when $n$ is infinite or for a specific value of $p$. In contrast, the study finds a non-zero value for the group $H$ under a particular condition. The study also explores the role of the commenitor ideal in the theory and its connection to the isomorphism types of the groups $G$ and $H$. The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in an overwhelming number of infections and deaths worldwide. In an effort to mitigate the virus's transmission, many countries have implemented contact tracing programs, employing both traditional and digital methods. The latter typically relies on mobile device data such as location, movement, and user interactions, often shared with government health authorities,, and, increasingly, with private companies. While contact tracing technology has been generally well-received, particularly during the pandemic, concerns have been raised about its implications for user data privacy and security. Given the proliferation of devices capable of revealing sensitive user information,, and the rising threat of data breaches, as witnessed in recent COVID-19 related leaks of user data, and, more critically still, the rising danger of unauthorized access to this information, as observed in 2020 with the exposure of sensitive information through the 'Coronav\'irus-SUS' data base, which includes private and health information of Brazilian users, we examine in this paper the extent to which contact tracing information can be compromised. Specifically, we look to investigate, using a novel COVID-19 model, the likelihood that user locations can be determined even when only rough data is provided, following a data breach, and whether this poses a significant enough threat to compromise overall data confidentiality when breached. Furthermore, we explore ways to estimate COVID-19 prevalence and total infected individuals using basic statistical methods, and show how an adversary can easily bypass these measures, and finally, we suggest potential countermeasures to mitigate the security risks associated with contact tracing information. Results obtained from numerical experiments using real-world data demonstrate the efficacy of proposed solutions. Using these findings, we argue that while contact tracing may remain a vital tool in the fight against COVID-19 and other diseases, its implementation must also prioritize data security and develop efficient methods to safeguard user information to ensure its continued effectiveness. This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems. The tool is built on the concept of a shallow embedding of C in ACL2. The process begins with the conversion of C functions into ACL2 functions using a translation system, which is then proof-checked in a separate ACL2 environment. The tool specializes in creating mutations, a key technique used in software security testing. It allows users to translate ACL2 test cases into C input data, allowing the assessment of software vulnerabilities. The tool's output comprises pairs of ACL2 functions and theorems, which validate the correctness of the C code. The tool's functionality was demonstrated through its application in developing a library for creating proof-trackable C code and the development of two ACL2-based proof-tracking techniques for complex software security issues. The tool was successfully used in the creation of a ACL2-based proof-tracking system for memory safety that utilizes memory access tracking. The resulting system's functionality was extensively tested, with the examination of its output providing valuable insights into its performance. The tool's limitations were also discussed, leading to proposed future research opportunities. The tool's source code and a sample dataset are available for public access. Estimating the pose of 3D objects is a crucial task in advanced computer vision and robotics applications. Although significant advancements have been made, current advanced methods still struggle with identifying and positioning 230+ object categories, mainly due to limited training data and class discrepancies. In response, we developed a novel, zero-shot object pose estimation framework based on category-level information only. By integrating a category embedding module, our method effectively utilizes word-level representations from language models to encode object classes. This results in substantial improvements when applied to the RGB and RGB-D domains, especially when dealing with rare and unseen categories, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by 8.5% and 5.9% respectively. Additionally, experiments demonstrate our method's adaptability to new categories and configurations, solidifying its potential as a versatile foundation for object pose estimation and other related applications. Evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that STAF achieves a superior accuracy-to-data-ratio compared to benchmarks. Furthermore, STAF's compact memory architecture and online learning capabilities enable autonomous adaptation to changing traffic patterns. As a result, STAF has the potential to become a practical and efficient solution for intelligent transportation systems. To circumvent this issue, we are exploring the use of symbolic-affective vectors that combine linguistic and affective characteristics, thereby facilitating cross-lingual retrieval. Our research is centered on developing a model that leverages the symbolic and affective interactions between English and a target non-English language to improve retrieval results. To this end, we are proposing two frameworks: a first one involves pre-training an English model with an ensemble of symbolic and affective transformers from multiple target languages, which enables interaction and potential knowledge sharing across these languages. A second, interactive framework involves iteratively fine-tuning the transformer for each target language, one at a time. To assess these models, we are utilizing a benchmark dataset with human-assessed scores from the WAKE dataset and four more recent datasets, demonstrating that both pre-trained and interactive models excel in symbolic-affective retrieval and outperform strong baselines, while the interactive model offers the quickest speed and the most efficient use of resources, especially when multiple target languages can be processed in parallel, which could potentially benefit cross-lingual symbolic-affective information retrieval applications. This study investigates the freeness, transcendence, and maximal orders of Toeplitz algebras with symbols from various function spaces over compact oval domains in terms of complex variables. To achieve this, the author constructs reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and establishes an asymptotic formula for the norm of Toeplitz operators, which relies on a novel Szegö integral formula. This formula not only facilitates the proof of a previously conjectured formula but also yields additional, novel results for Bergman spaces and general reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, along with an extension of the classical Hartogs' theorem. Ultimately, the results derived from Szegö's work on essential norms of Toeplitz operators also hold significance in this context. These findings lead to Freiman-type theorems for Toeplitz algebras with symbols belonging to $L^{\infty}$ over oval domains with smooth boundaries, and also extend a previously established theorem of Widom to the realm of Toeplitz series. Additional applications to $\mathbb{C}^n$ domains are also proposed for future exploration. The study culminates in a novella-length conclusion that draws upon Szegö's work and provides an extensive, in-depth analysis of the topic. One critical element impacting the results of Neural Architecture Search (NAS) is the synergy between different components in the search space. Various NAS methods treat these interactions with indifference, which, as investigated in this paper, hampers the architecture search outcome. To illuminate these connections, a mathematical model was created to measure the influence between cells in the search space. Experiment results show that this synergy has a substantial impact on NAS, as disregarding these interactions picks top-ranked cells only 29.2% of the time. Based on these insights, a search space design is proposed that minimizes these synergy effects, in conjunction with an efficient random search method to counter these interactions. As shown in the experiment results, this approach leads to a substantial boost in the top-1 accuracy of architectures searched (e.g. boosting MobileNet to  82.2 from  78.8). Traditional methods for evaluating the dependability of translators involve comprehensive case studies and expert assessment. This approach has significant drawbacks, as case studies are time-consuming to conduct, and expert judgment can be influenced by personal biases. In contrast, Bayesian translation evaluation provides a more precise and objective way to evaluate dependability. This method constructs a reliability scale using a reference framework, measures translation accuracy for a given text, and calculates a dependability index. Unlike traditional methods, Bayesian translation evaluation only requires data analysis, eliminating the need for case studies or expert judgment. This innovative approach was successfully applied to evaluate the dependability of two translators in a real-world context. The results showed that the dependability indices for Translator A and Translator B were 0.82 and 0.79, respectively. The approach yielded precise and objective results, free from biases, highlighting its potential as a viable evaluation method. We've found evidence that suggests the much-publicized lottery ticket phenomenon in deep neural networks can, in fact, be attributed to specific structures within certain networks, rather than being a universal pattern applicable to all neural networks. Our study specifically examined the characteristics of the best-performing sub-networks from a fully-connected MNIST model and a convolutional MNIST model, discovering some intriguing patterns. Interestingly, the best-performing sub-networks from the fully-connected model exhibited a much broader range of sizes, both in terms of number of parameters and number of units, when compared to those of the convolutional model. Moreover, the best-performing sub-networks from the latter exhibited far more consistent and predictable patterns, both in terms of structure and performance, which could potentially be attributed to the inherent properties of the model itself. These discoveries led us to conclude that the lottery ticket phenomenon, at least in this context, appears to be largely influenced by factors such as architecture and data type. Moreover, the fact that the best-performing sub-networks from the convolutional model exhibited a high degree of compactness and determinism also raises questions regarding a purportedly prevalent phenomenon within neural networks, namely that of "trimming": a supposed ability to trim down the complexity of neural networks. Our study offers a novel perspective on this concept, suggesting instead that the best-performing sub-networks from the convolutional model exhibited more consistent and predictable patterns as a result of selecting out "noisy" units through the process of pruning, effectively "trimming" down the noise. These discoveries hold broader implications for the understanding of neural network behavior and encourage further study into the characteristics of lottery ticket phenomenon, particularly in terms of its relationship to neural network architecture and "trimming". This work presents my technical report on the NeurIPS 2022 Visual Domain Adaptation Competition challenge solutions, where I emerged as the first-place contender across all three tasks. At the core of my approach is a general, efficient framework for domain adaptation that can be readily enhanced with MIMO techniques. To solve this task efficiently and quickly, I developed a two-step strategy. The first step leverages an unsupervised domain adaptation method, and the second incorporates MIMO techniques. To account for domain ambiguity in the second step, I integrated a variational autoencoder. Furthermore, I developed two MIMO techniques and two options for the second step of my approach. Through an extensive analysis of different combinations of these components, I identified the configuration leading to the highest accuracy and submitted it as my solution to the first two challenge tasks. Ultimately, this solution yielded 100% accuracy on the test data for task 3, and I obtained the top performance in all challenge tasks, securing first-place rankings across the board. Notably, our solution effectively handles large-scale problems, and it can handle data with a size of 32 million pixels without encountering memory issues. Moreover, our solution's execution time is highly competitive, amounting to the following time:
  - Two-step MIMO adaptation: 2.5 hours (step 1) + 2.5 hours (step 2)
  - Two-step MIMO adaptation with VAE: 2.5 hours (step 1) + 3.5 hours (step 2)
where the times were estimated using the average results from multiple runs. To resolve task 1, I employed the two-step MIMO adaptation method. Initially, I utilized the domain adaptation technique, and then I applied the MIMO techniques, starting with MIMO 1 and MIMO 2 in successive iterations. The first iteration of the two-step MIMO adaptation method led to an accuracy of 85.71%, and the second iteration resulted in an accuracy of 89.29%. For task 2, I leveraged the two-step MIMO adaptation method with VAE. The accuracy of the first iteration was 85.71%, and the accuracy of the second iteration was 89.29%. The results for task 3 were not provided as the report was submitted before the challenge deadline, and I could only report the final accuracy of 100% for this task upon re-running the code multiple times. The code and findings are accessible via the link https://github.com/AsadKarim

t-SNE is a popular, in-depth dimensionality reduction technique with wide application across machine learning and data visualization. It's designed primarily for linear data, with the majority of its research focusing on spherical data through the use of vector means. This approach, though, is flawed because vector means are biased by the data's high dimensions, making t-SNE's effective recovery of nearby data points on a low-dimensional sphere highly conditional. We show that minimizing pairwise log-probability distances in t-SNE is equivalent to minimizing a weighted sum of the data's vector's dot products, equivalent to minimizing a weighted version of the data's Newton polytope's circumsphere's radius. Based on this, we developed VMF-SNE, a novel, unbiased t-SNE variation that increases the data's spikiness and provides a more precise reconstruction of nearby data points on a low-dimensional sphere. It also avoids the t-SNE's overexpansion by not minimizing the spherical shell's width, achieved through the use of the convex hull's unique property of having its apex lying on the Newton polytope's circumsphere. Our visualization experiments show that VMF-SNE offers notable improvements over the classical t-SNE. Our study also proposes a spherical extension of the popular Scikit-learn library's t-SNE implementation. Implementation is available at https://github.com/kr-lab/vmf-tnsne.
