Ultimately, our study emphasizes the need for a standardized approach to detect and eradicate test odors, as well as a greater emphasis on communication among developers to achieve this goal. 
Our research contributes to software engineering by shedding light on a previously under-studied topic, providing empirical evidence and practical recommendations for addressing test odors. 
Lastly, we outline potential future research directions inspired by our study's findings. This paper explores the existence and uniqueness of solutions to inclusion problems that incorporate the grinding (sweeping) of sets and points. It essentially represents a system of differential equations with the grinding of sets applied to the velocity and acceleration components. Considering that these equations contain elements of point grinding that aren't necessarily convex, which can lead to the grinding of the zero set with a compact set, and due to the irregularity of the grinding maps, analyzing the local Lipschitz property along the obtained trajectories poses a significant challenge. To address this, the research establishes and proves a new regularity property of the grinding maps and uses it to demonstrate that an appropriate modified version of the Cauchy problem has a unique solution with a residual term. This modified problem is then used to demonstrate the local Lipschitz property along the trajectories of the original sweeping problem for nonconvex sets with unbounded grinding. Ultimately, the results are applied to model a mass-dampers-system on a rigid base, where an existence and uniqueness theorem for the measure-valued solution is demonstrated. Our work also shows that a measure-valued solution can take the form of a classical solution under certain conditions, and we derive a first-order necessary condition for a measure-valued solution in the form of a variational inequality involving the grazing phenomenon. This research develops a probabilistic approach to a method for tensor singular value decomposition (TSVD) based on random projections. We derive an efficient formula for estimating TSVD core and singular tensors, determining the number of passes through the data required for low-norm noise suppression, and establish a bound on the 2-norm of residual error. Under noiseless conditions, the proposed method can exactly recover the singular tensors by a number of passes proportional to the number of data samples from a tensor, the number of elements in each sample, and the logarithm of the tensor rank. We demonstrate that our approach can compete with existing stochastic methods for TSVD, achieving superior performance in several tensor decomposition tasks for three different types of singular values. Our experiments incorporate various types of tensors (image plates, random tensors, and tensors from a steerable filter approach), multiple ranks, and diverse noise models. Additionally, the proposed method is adapted to a probabilistic version of stochastic multi-dimensional singular value decomposition (MDSVDD) by generalizing the formula and providing an optional number of passes formula for MDSVDD. We compare the performance of our method with the currently fastest methods for MDSVDD, achieving lower average 2-norm residual errors in all cases. Our research also documents the development of a highly optimized, multithreaded C++ code for MDSVDD based on numerical tensor operations, the TTN project. This software enables the demonstration of the efficacy of the proposed methods through rapid tensor computations. In accordance with our findings, the provided code is made freely available to the community over GitHub. Our work has culminated in the development of highly optimized, general-purpose C++ code for TSVD, MDSVDD, and related tensor operations, the TTN project, the steerable image filter library, and the SwinTSVD steerable image filter approach. In various fields, neighborhood-based initiatives to share COVID-19 infection data have been launched, aiming to boost the efficiency of contact tracing operations. Despite their growing influence, the extent to which these local tracing efforts augment the traditional tracing strategy employed by public health authorities remains unclear. To answer this question, a study was carried out to compare the validity and reach of COVID-19 infection data in England, both from the standard contact tracing service and local tracing initiatives, from their inception in May 2021 until their termination in March 2022. To achieve this, a study was conducted on self-reported, user-generated data retrieved from the GitHub platform, which provided valuable insights into the local tracing efforts. According to the findings, the different tracing methods generated distinct sets of COVID-19 infection data. Offloading, a widely utilized technique to reduce the size of data, was found to be instrumental in the local tracing efforts. From a broader perspective, the study has shed light on the critical factors that govern the adoption and effectiveness of contact tracing efforts, which are instrumental in containing COVID-19 outbreaks. These factors can be categorized into three primary groups: (1) technical considerations, related to the privacy and dynamic configuration of infection data; (2) social aspects, characterized by social dynamics and human interactions; and (3) policy-related elements, driven by the decision-making processes of public health authorities and the general public. Based on these key factors, several general recommendations were proposed, which can be applied both during pandemic-related emergencies and non-emergency periods to ensure the successful deployment of contact tracing efforts. These recommendations include establishing a common understanding among stakeholders about the inherent limitations and purposes of contact tracing services, fostering a culture of transparency and reciprocal social behavior, and providing individuals with sufficient information to make informed decisions, among other policy interventions. Ultimately, the study has provided valuable insights into the design and mitigation strategies of COVID-19

We're focusing on learning reverse skills, which means acquiring a set of
movement patterns by watching someone else perform tasks in a complex
environment and then doing the reverse action to maintain the observer's
balance. The key to this is to define a constraint that ensures the agent
moves in the opposite direction of the observed actions. Once this constraint
is in place, we can use reinforcement learning to fine-tune our approach.
Our method doesn't require detailed information about the tasks or the system
dynamic models. By combining this with techniques for reducing noise and
disorderly movements, we can learn reverse skills through self-practice and also
achieve expertise in tasks like stabilizing other objects, all without
depending on external rewards, so long as the target is identified correctly. 
Our computer simulations show that our method is successful in a variety of
tasks and allows for effortless transfer to different scenarios, confirming
that it is possible to develop a set of general movement skills that can be
applied in many situations. 
Furthermore, we tested our method using a sophisticated robotic setup, which
involved balancing a ball on a moving turntable, and found that our method is
successful in a real-world environment as well. 
Overall, our findings open up a new area of study, which is learning reverse
skills, and suggest that learning can be just as efficient as teaching. 
The code used for these experiments can be accessed at https://github.com/harvardai/Reverse-Skill-Learning.

We introduce a methodology to separately estimate the error of physics-based neural network predictions. This method relies on generalized loss functions, incorporates prior knowledge about the data, and leverages analytical error estimation. Utilizing the Bayesian framework, our approach assesses the reliability of predictions made by physics-enabled neural networks by analyzing the uncertainty associated with their outputs. Furthermore, our analytical error estimation results in a closed-form expression of the expected error, which can be optimized in conjunction with the loss function to refine the model's accuracy. Our numerical evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in estimating prediction errors, particularly in complex problems requiring method remapping and mesh refinement. This method's source code is publicly available to facilitate its use. Our study provides novel insights into the behavior of physics-informed neural networks under the Bayesian framework, offering a potential means to enhance the reliability and accuracy of AI-driven simulations. Additionally, we explore the possibility of applying this method to other neural networks lacking explicit physical constraints, albeit with limited success. Despite these encouraging findings, we caution that the reliance of our approach on prior knowledge may impose stringent requirements on the quality of input data. Our study provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the behavior of physics-informed neural networks within the Bayesian framework and sheds light on the crucial role of analytical error estimation in AI-driven simulations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the incorporation of analytical error estimation can facilitate generalizable learning, particularly in complex problems beyond the scope of our present analysis. Nevertheless, we anticipate that the incorporation of sensory input, characterized by implicit knowledge, will enable the reliable estimation of prediction errors for a broader class of problems, including those without explicit physical constraints. To this end, we have developed an alternative approach to error estimation, albeit one that shows more limited results in our current experiments. A detailed explanation of the theoretical formulation and numerical evaluation of our approach, as well as the associated public software repository and problem files, are provided at the end of this contribution. This study reviews the advancements in modeling atmospheric contamination for the advancement of epidemiological research, blending geostatistics and advanced signal processing techniques. The focus will lie on past developments, current challenges, and potential future pathways at the intersection of statistical modeling and artificial intelligence.  Building upon previous work, we will examine two key aspects:  first, the spatial modeling of atmospheric pollution with geostatistics, and second, the integration of machine learning for addressing the inaccuracies and uncertainties associated with atmospheric measurement tools, such as CO sensors.  Ultimately, we will highlight promising avenues of research at the interface of machine intelligence and statistical modeling for the effective analysis of air quality and epidemiological data.  Specifically, we will explore deep learning-based methods for the rapid detection of air quality changes, personalized risk assessment, and urban planning strategies all aimed at mitigating the health impacts of atmospheric pollution.  The discussed concepts and techniques will be exemplified with case studies from Mexico City and other locations.  This research was conducted in the context of the Universidad Autonoma de Ciudad Juarez's ITM research group efforts.  Specifically, we have developed methods for the recovery of atmospheric measurement series using advanced signal processing and geometric analysis, and are now working on a systematic risk assessment framework for the most vulnerable populations, to be achieved through the development of customized risk models.  Our work at the Universidad Autonoma de Ciudad Juarez's ITM research group has focused on the application of geostatistics and machine learning for the analysis of atmospheric contamination and epidemiological data.  The outcomes of this research have been successfully transported to the city of Chihuahua as part of the Air Quality Monitoring and Epidemiological Research Project, an initiative led by the university.  In this project, we are using geostatistical and machine learning techniques to improve the monitoring and understanding of atmospheric quality in the city, and to develop new strategies to communicate risk information to the public and decision makers.  Ultimately, to further contribute to the analysis of air quality and epidemiological data, we are developing a collaborative framework that integrates the efforts and expertise of researchers from the fields of artificial intelligence and statistical modeling to work towards the development of more effective methods for the detection of air quality changes, personalized risk assessments, and urban planning strategies all aimed at reducing the health impacts of atmospheric pollution.  The promising outcomes of this research efforts have the potential to significantly contribute to the development of more effective air quality monitoring systems and to ultimately protect the health of the most vulnerable populations from the harmful effects of atmospheric pollution.

We introduce OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation for illustrating connections between entities in extensive, detailed knowledge frameworks. We pinpointed shortcomings in current interactive visualisation tools designed for ontologies, specifically their inadequate handling of complex hierarchical structures and numerous, detailed relationships. We devised OntoPlot as a non-linear, graphical display that effectively shows links between entities, highlighting those with the most connections. This visualisation makes it easy to identify clusters of related concepts, even in large knowledge frameworks, making it perfect for exploring vast datasets, understanding complex concepts consisting of multiple subcomponents, and reviewing changes to knowledge frameworks over time. We implemented a prototype of OntoPlot using Dooven, a knowledge framework dedicated to everyday objects, but our method can be applied to any large knowledge framework with extensive, detailed information. We observed substantial improvements in performance when optimising OntoPlot's implementation for Dooven, a strategy that can be replicated when working with other large knowledge frameworks. The results of our experiments demonstrate that OntoPlot is easy to navigate, providing response times of under 0.1 seconds, even when interacting with large knowledge frameworks consisting of 50000 concepts. We firmly believe that OntoPlot has the potential to be an effective and easy-to-use visualisation tool for researchers working with large knowledge frameworks. We introduce a novel technique to address the issue of training fully supervised automatic speech recognition models with inter-domain constraints. Our approach leverages CycleGAN to translate inter-domain penalty signals into domain-specific representations, which are then combined with the original target domain speeches to create a more effective training dataset. This extended dataset is used to train an automatic speech recognition model with enhanced inter-domain penalty regularization, ultimately leading to improved speech recognition accuracy. Our method demonstrates exceptional performance with minimal unlabelled speech data, achieving a word error rate of 6.24% with 1 hour of unlabelled speech, significantly outperforming the baseline with 9.15% word error rate. Furthermore, we observe that the cycle-consistent translations provide qualitatively coherent translations and data augmentation effects, revealing the previously underexplored relationships between speech, language, and acoustic-gesture domains. Our work highlights the potential of leveraging CycleGAN to bridge domain gaps and inter-domain penalty signals to extract rich domain-specific information. Moreover, this research offers an innovative perspective on the use of Inter-domain penalty regularization for automatic speech recognition. It also expands the current understanding of domain translation and interpolation techniques to enhance training data quality. Finally, it demonstrates an efficient and accurate method for automatic speech recognition training with varying degrees of supervision. (i) With a large amount of unlabelled data, our approach performs similarly to a fully supervised baseline, indicating robustness in data-rich environments. (ii) In a semi-supervised setting, our method exhibits high performance with a relatively small amount of labelled data and large amounts of unlabelled data. (iii) In a low-data regime with minimal supervision, our approach displays high resilience despite the significant domain gap and extreme class imbalance present in the data. It is worth noting that our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/asharakeh/cyclgan-interdomain-penalties. Our work has the potential to be significantly expanded into the development of inter-domain penalty regularization for diverse speech tasks, as well as domain-adversarial neural machine translation. Furthermore, the automatic speech detection framework presented in this study differs from the domain-adversarial neural machine translation paradigm. As a result, the robot develops an internal prediction mechanism that is not influenced by external factors, allowing it to seamlessly integrate its self-awareness with external sensor data, which is then utilized to create an accurate and detailed environmental model. By integrating a dedicated learning mechanism into its energy-based navigation system, the robot is able to efficiently balance exploration and exploitation, which is then reflected in its learning behavior as measured by the Loss function over time. To simulate authentic throwing motions without actually throwing, we used a collection of simulated trajectories. Our analysis revealed that despite an increase in incorrect calls with distorted throwing mechanics, the point of release particularly affects the perception of the type of pitch and the distance the ball travels. Moreover, observer accuracy on the point of release is better correlated with the ball's maximum height than its trajectory duration. Recent advances in Natural Language Processing (NLP) have led to remarkable improvements in Image Captioning, with many methods fine-tuning pre-trained language models with image data to generate descriptive outputs. However, given diverse requirements and use cases, traditional fine-tuning techniques are often problematic as they expose the model to sensitive or unwanted information, potentially compromising its performance and trustworthiness. Consequentialism in AI decision-making is a widely accepted ethical guideline, but it has been challenging to define a concept of harm that aligns with intuitive human understanding. Previous AI research focused on harm primarily from the perspective of consequence, ignoring its causal structure and assuming damage results from a combination of actions and conditions. In this study, we challenge this approach and propose a more nuanced model based on causal concepts. By distinguishing cause and disablement, we identify the fundamental elements of harm and outline the criteria for identifying an agent's actions as harmful. Our framework, with its emphasis on causal relationships and enabling effects, expands the scope of harm to unintended consequences and considers policies as potential causes of harm. In contrast to the traditional view, we find that harm is not solely a product of actions but can also be caused by maintaining or removing certain conditions. Moreover, we expand the concept of harm to cover the maintenance of adverse conditions, denoting this as 'harm by maintenance.' Our investigation of the formal properties of this theory, with its eight primitive properties, reveals the intricate characteristics of harm and their connections. In the second part of this study, we explore the possibilities of representing the causal concepts of harmenability, with its twelve binary properties and one universal property. Based on these properties, we identify the complete language of a model theory and use this to describe and classify different types of conditions, with our method potentially applied to other domain classifications. Finally, we demonstrate that the causal concepts of harmenability can be effectively reduced to the resulting harm framework, with our reduction preserving the logical connections between these concepts, offering a simplified and unified understanding of harmenability and harm. In the third part of this study, we apply the tools and concepts developed from our analysis to a range of AI policy domains, with our method, with steps, capable of identifying the causes of harmenability in these domains, offering a benchmark for assessing the ethical consequences of policies and conditions. Our model, with its application of the harmenability properties, can determine the least enabling conditions required to identify an agent's actions as harmful, with the tools and concepts developed from our analysis ready for implementation in AI systems. With our system, with its application of the harmenability properties, capable of describing the causal structure of harmenability in a graphical format, we are now in a position to expand the existing collection of ethical AI frameworks, with our collection of the harmenability properties, with their reduction to the harm theory, offering a unified understanding of the concept of harmenability

Vertebral body identification through CT scans is critical in both research and clinical settings for assessment and quantification of spinal degeneration, as well as detecting spinal abnormalities. However, vertebras in CT images often become distorted due to postural changes, which poses an obstacle to developing fully automated detection and quantification methods. This study presents a novel approach to vertebral recognition in fully three-dimensional and posturally adapted CT scans. By manually marking the centerline of the spine and using a customized fitting template, the transition from two-dimensional to three-dimensional is seamlessly transitioned from two-dimensional to three-dimensional. A nearest neighbor search is then employed to identify vertebras based on characteristic features. Due to variations in vertebral shape and shape, the model is instead trained using vertebral cross-sections' morphological characteristics, thereby facilitating robust vertebral identification under various postural conditions. A comprehensive dataset including multiple postures, acquired under different conditions, is used to validate the accuracy of the method, demonstrating exceptional performance with an overall mean distance between predicted vertebral contours and ground truth of 0.36 millimeters, along with an 0.93 area under the curve measure in terms of F1-score. Compared to the existing approaches, the proposed method demonstrates a significant improvement of 15% in edge localization and vertebral body detection. This technique has the potential to be applied seamlessly in three-dimensional CT scans, thereby paving the development of automated spinal degeneration quantification and abnormality detection methods. Researchers have carried out in-depth simulations of a local tearing instability in a slab plasma with a single-species particle approach. They specifically examined the microscale dynamics of the tearing mechanism in lab-generated and solar type III radio bursts. By simulation, they numerically solved the electron dispersion relation in the vicinity of an initial current sheet perturbation. These simulations, extending to micron scales, showed that the electron response dominates, resulting in distinct separations forming along magnetic field lines. These separations grew exponentially, tearing the magnetic field apart. They found the tearing rate sensitive to the magnetic shear angle, but not to the level of nearby electron heating. Unlike earlier macroscopic studies, this microscopic dynamics relied on electron nonlinearities, not fluid dynamics, and thus differs from previously studied larger-scale dynamics. They have further observed that the exponential growth of the tearing instability in microns and above is likely caused by an earlier phase of electron thermodynamics. This process is believed to be a common mechanism underlying both lab-generated and solar type III radio bursts. This small-scale tearing instability is thought to contribute to the formation of plasma bubbles and transverse structures observed in these phenomena. It may also be an early forming instability, along with others, that shape and influence plasma bubble formation and spatial structures. They have observed that these plasma bubbles likely result from combinations of multiple processes, including local and global factors. Understanding these mechanisms requires a high level of spatial resolution and dynamic range. Studying and interpreting these processes, therefore, demands similar levels of consideration. In particular, this small-scale tearing is likely followed by larger-scale nonlinear processes, including slapping, electron weightlifting, and turbulent cascade. In contrast to these mechanisms, there exists little or no small-scale tearing beyond micron scales in collisional plasmas. In these cases, plasma bubble formation is likely attributed to the plasma bubble formation mechanisms other than small-scale tearing. They have observed that mechanisms such as electron gravity nonlinearities, plasma bubble formation, and turbulent cascade are more likely responsible. In general, a hierarchical classification of mechanisms by their spatial scales, as well as their underlying physical processes, is proposed. In turn, this may yield better understanding and more reliable interpretations of plasma processes, including those at small, large, and all scales. In the world of fashion, where images of outfits are abundant, retrieving images with similar styles can be a daunting task, especially when styles keep evolving rapidly. This paper presents a novel approach to fashion image retrieval by exploiting a lesser known field in computer vision: vision and psychology. By linking a given fashion image to a specific style, our method aims to retrieve images with the exact same attributes as those originally paired. These attributes can be manipulative such as dress color or confinement of garments, which are difficult to handle using traditional methods. To address this, we developed a semi-supervised technique that levels up feature manipulation to the item and not just the overall style level. This involves categorizing attributes into wearable and non wearable ones to boost feature quality and control. Additionally, using a fusion of two different training strategies, our method boosts performance and flexibility by simultaneously training a model to move features around and one to move images based on labels. Experimental results show that our approach significantly boosts performance and controls over wearable attributes while surpassing state-of-the-art practices with 8% increased accuracy above FashionIQ. This improved performance allows us to apply our method to a wide range of computer vision and fashion challenges. The existing Dual Gradient Descent algorithm is built upon penality methods, with a penality term based on the dual norm of the constraint function, making it a versatile method adaptable to diverse constraints. To improve its performance, the DGD method can be enhanced with a convergence rate guarantee similar to that of non-smooth optimization algorithms. The proposed algorithm provides both stability in the presence of noise and optimal convergence rates for strong convex optimization problems, even when the constraint function is not differentiable. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the penality method in resolving ill-posed problems, particularly for data reconstruction and inverse problems. Due to its simplicity, penality methods are suitable for high-dimensional constraints, whereas other algorithms may struggle with computational or informational limitations. Penality methods can be viewed as a specific type of Tikhonov method where the regularizer is based on the dual norm of the constraint, offering a connection to Tikhonov regularization, particularly for inverse problems in the complex domain where the regularizer can be expressed in terms of the Hessian tensor. In recent years, the deployment of Battery-powered IEEE 802.11n Extenders has become a widespread practice in residential and commercial settings to enhance WiFi coverage. Since these devices operate without a power source, they often consume energy from the connected Access Point (AP) when connected, which may cause network outages when the AP's bandwidth capacity is fully occupied with Extender power demands. To prevent this, we propose a solution that incorporates IEEE 802.11k/v standards to prioritize and configure AP/Extender relationships based on specific criteria such as link quality and AP capacity. By leveraging these standards, we can establish and maintain AP/Extener associations that minimize network outages, which is the focus of our research. The proposed work suggests an optimal AP/Extener configuration strategy that reduces network outages to zero, to the best of our knowledge, for the first time. The method works by prioritizing and optimizing AP/Extener configuration based on channel load and uses the IEEE 802.11k/v standard's association classes and measurement tools for this purpose. The main idea behind this technique is to assign each AP/Extener pair a score based on its available backhaul connections and configure them in order of priority, starting with the pair with the least score, to ensure that only pairs with available backhaul capacity are configured. The method also employs feedback and reevaluation functions to maintain and update the AP/Extener configuration every time the network or one of the APs changes, which helps ensure minimal network outages. The technique bears similarities with the Max Weight Scheduling Algorithm, where the value of each AP/Extener pair depends on its link quality and available bandwidth, and the configuration is made based on the maximum value, which helps in optimizing the AP/Extener configuration, and hence, reduces network outages to the minimum. The technique's feasibility has been validated using simulations, which demonstrate its potential in reducing network outages to the minimum, and the actual deployment is also being planned. The planned deployment will help in evaluating the technique's performance in real-world settings and the actual outcomes will be reported. The technique has the potential to be widely applicable not only to IEEE 802.11n but also to the next generation of IEEE 802.11ac and IEEE 802.11ax standards, and the technique might also be useful in other relevant use cases, which will be investigated in the near future.
